(UNEP) report has pointed out that a thick brown haze forms over India 
101 

RAJYA SABHA [29 November, 2002] 
and much of Asia, containing ash, acids, aerosols and other particles, which 
could have profound effect on human health, crop-yield and the rain pattern; 
(b) if so, the details in this regard and how far it would pollute air in our 
land; 
(c) the details of the major observations/conclusions contained in the report 
and the result of any further investigations made into these conclusions; and 
(d) the steps taken by Government to guard against the harmful effects on 
our system? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI TR. BAALU): 
(a) to (d) An international collaborative study "Indian Ocean Research 
Experiment (INDOEX)" has indicated haze over the Indian Ocean. The haze 
is not a permanent feature of the atmosphere over the Asian region and the 
surrounding seas. It occurs only during January—March, the season in which 
INDOEX observations were made in 1999. Conclusive data are not available 
to co-relate the impact of haze on human health as well as the monsoon and/or 
agriculture of our country. The United Nations Environment Programme 
(UNEP) has, this year, brought out a report entitled "The Asian Brown Cloud: 
Climate and other Environmental Impacts" based on INDOEX. The press 
release of the UNEP launching the said report paints an alarming picture of 
the impacts of this haze on both regional and global scales. However, most of 
the concerns expressed therein are not well substantiated by reliable modeling 
studies or experimental observations. The existing legal and policy 
framework, supported by several initiatives to protect and improve the 
environment, addresses the concerns of air pollution in the country.

1115. SHRI KAILASH JOSHI: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT AND 
FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) when was the Ganga Action Plan started; 
(b) what are the details of tortuous attempts made to clean the Gang^ and the

for the purpose; and 
(e) by when the report is likely to be presented? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. BAALU) 
(a) and (b) The Ganga Action Plan (GAP) has been taken up in two phases. The 
first phase of Ganga Action Plan was started in 1985 with the objective of 
preventing the pollution of river Ganga and to improve its water quality along 
25 towns. The Plan was completed on 31.3.2000 and an amount of Rs. 451.70 
crore has been spent. Against a target capacity of 873 million litres per day 
(mid) planned for treatment of wastewater, a capacity to treat 865 mid has been. 
created. 
The GAP Phase-Il, which covers Ganga and its tributaries viz. Yamuna, Gomti 
115 

RAJYA SABHA [29 November, 2002] 
and Damodar was approved in phases between 1993 and 1996 and is under 
implementation. Out of an approved cost of Rs. 1498.86 crore, an amount of 
Rs. 732.80 crore has been spent and a capacity to treat 724 mid of wastewater 
has been created so far. The GAP Phas e-II is targeted for completion by 
December, 2005. 
(c) A comprehensive evaluation of GAP Phase-I by independent agencies 
(universities and R&D institutions) was undertaken in April, 1995. The 
evaluation report concluded that reduction of discharge of organic matter, a 
necessary first step in restoring the water quality of the river, has been achieved 
to a fair level under GAP Phase-I. Concern was expressed about contamination 
of the river with bacterial pollution and the need to address the same. However, 
it was stated that GAP Phase-I as conceived and implemented is an appropriate 
programme for application to other river basins. The shortcomings of the 
programme have also been brought out in the report and have been taken note 
of for modification in the subsequent programmes. 
On the directions of the Planning Commission, a Cost Benefit Analysis of 
Ganga Action Plan was carried out in 1995-96 by the Harvard Institute of 
International Development, U.K. in collaboration with reputed national institutes, 
the Study demonstrated that: 
(i) inspite of its many shortcomings, the Ganga Action Plan has delivered 
significant benefits to India and there have been improvements in water 
quality (measured in terms of dissolved oxygen and bio-chemical oxygen 
demand) in some places. The polluted stretch of the river violating the 
bathing class standard, which would have been atleast 740 kms. between 
Kannauj and Varanasi without GAP Phase-1 had been reduced to 437 
kms. after completion of GAP Phase-I. 
(ii) both users and non-users have benefited and the result is that the real 
rate of return on GAP Phase-I is well above the 10% required of public 
sector projects. 
(iii) in terms of both the cost involved and the time taken, Ganga Action 
Plan compared favourably with other clean-up programmes undertaken 
In the world for rivers Thames, Rhine and Danube. 
The Central Pollution Control Board, on the directions of the Suprqm«sCourt, 
carried out a detailed inspection of the sewage treatment plants (STPs) set up 
under GAP ;Phase-l in July, 2001. The Inspection Report of the Central Pollution 
Control Board concluded that out of the 35 STPs sanctioned under GAP 
116 

[29 November, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
Phase-I, 32 were commissioned and of these 29 were found flinctioning. The 
report also indicates that adequate ftind allocation for operation and maintenance 
of STPs is not provided, particularly in Bihar and UP. 
(d) and (e) The Japan International Cooperation Agency of the Government 
of Japan has recently agreed to provide technical assistance for taking up a 
development study on 'Water Quality Management Plan for river Ganga'. The 
objective of the study is to (i) formulate the Master Plan for water quality 
management for the Ganga basin concerning liquid waste, and (ii) formulate 
feasibility studies for high priority projects identified in the Master Plan focusing 
on four towns namely, Kanpur, Allahabad, Varanasi and Lucknow. This study is 
different than the three studies mentioned in para (c) above as it aims at 
formulating the remaining works to be taken up over and above those 
implemented/proposed to be implemented under GAP Phase-! and II in the four 
towns in the Ganga Basin. It will take two years to complete the study.

(b) and (c) The steps being taken to improve the literacy rate are as

(I) A new scheme of Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA) has been started for 
Universalization of Elementary Education in a mission mode with a 
district focus. SSA is to provide useful and relevant Elementary 
Education for all children in the 6—14 age group by 2010. The goals 
are as follows: 
* All children in school, Education Guarantee Scheme Centre, 
Alternate   School, 'Back-to-School' camps by 2003. 
* All children complete five years primary education by 2007. 
* All children complete eight years of schooling by 2010. 
* Focus on elementary education of satisfactory quality with emphasis 
on education for life. 
* Bridge all gender and social gaps at primary stage by 2007 and at 
elementary education level by 2010. 
* Universal retention by 2010. 
National Literacy Mission (MLM) seeks to attain full literacy, i.e. a 
sustainable threshold level of 75 per cent by 2005. It seeks to achieve this 
goal by imparting functional literacy to non-literates in 15^35 year age group. 
Major thrust of the programme is on promotion of literacy among women. In 
the literacy programmes, 60% of the le arners are women and around 60% of 
volunteers also are women and young girls. 
Various facets of literacy related backwardness like low female literacy, 
SC/ST literacy etc. are being addressed through the above-mentioned efforts.

Deemed University Status for Private Technical and Non-Technical 
Institutes 
1143. SHRl R.P. GOENKA : Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether h is a fact that a large number of private technical and non-
technical institutes, that have mushroomed across the country, have requested 
for grant of Deemed University status; 
(b) if so, the details of these institutions, State*wise and the action taken/ 
proposed to be taken on their requests; and 
(c) the details of guidelines laid down for maintaining objectivity in 
evaluating the private institutes for grant of the required status and the role 
assigned therefor to the UGC and the AICTE? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT [DR. (SHRIMATI) RITA VERMA]: (a) and (b) Various 
institutions have applied for grant of Deemed to be University status. A list 
of such institutions is annexed as statement (See below). Declaration of an 
institution as Deemed University is a statutory process done on fulfillment of 
several requirements under the guidelines. 
(c) Proposals for Deemed University status are examined in consultation 
with UGC and AICTE. UGC and AICTE have laid down the guidelines for 
considering the proposals for declaring an institution as Deemed to be 
University. These guidelines, inler-alia, provide that an institution should 
generally be: 
(i) Engaged in teaching programmes and research in chosen fields of 
specialisation which are innovative and very high academic 
standards at the Master's (or equivalent) and/or research levels. It 
should also have a greater interface with society through extra 
mural, extension and field action related programmes. 
(ii) Making in its areas of specialisation, distinct contribution to the 
objectives of the University education system through innovative 
programmes and on being recognised as a university capable of 
further enriching the university system as well as strengthening 
teaching and research in the institution and particularly in its area 
of specialisation. 
(iii)   Competent to undertake application-oriented programmes in 
emerging areas which are relevant and useful to various 
development sectors and to the society in general. 145 

RAJYA SABHA [29 November. 2002] 
(iv) Institutions should have the necessary viabihty and a management 
capable of contributing to the university ideals and traditions, 
Ordinarily, institutions affiliated to university and which are offering only 
conventional degree programmes leading to BA/B.Com/B.Sc. or MA/M.Com/ 
M.Sc, will not be considered for grant of deemed to be university status. 
However, such institution which is also offering innovative programmes, and 
which has adequate resources, might be considered for recognition as a 
university. Supplementary assistance for innovation may be considered by 
the UGC only in such exceptional cases.  
Institutions which are imparling routine type of instruction to full-time 
students or offering training programmes for in-service personnel, unless of 
high quality, would, generally, not qualify for recognition. 
In selective cases, outstanding research institutions specialising in Social 
Sciences, Sciences and Technology can be considered for research degree 
and highly specialised programmes at the Master's level. 
In case the institution is offering a degree/diploma, in professional 
subject(s), the acacdemic programme(s) should be recognised by the 
concerned statutory authority e.g. All India Council for Technical Education 
(AiCTE), Medical Council of India (MCI). Dental Council of India (DCI), 
Central Council of Homoeopathy (CCH), Indian Nursing Council (INC) etc. 
before it applies for a deemed to be university status under Section 3 of the 
UGC Act. 
This shall, however, not apply to de-novo institutions in the emerging 
areas with the promise of excellence, not yet fulfilling the prescribed guidelines 
of the UGC whose case will be considered for a provisional status for a 
Deemed to be University.

Commission are as under: 
155 

RAJYA SABHA [29 November, 2002] 
(1) A minimum of 51% of the Government equity may be given to 
employees (both present and past) of RITES. Government may retain 
25% of the equity. Balance equity may be distributed among reputed 
infrastructure consultancy organisation and infrastructure leasing and 
financing organisations after suitable pre-qualification. 
00 The Railways should have an agreement with RITES under which 
continuous induction of talented Railway personnel would be 
guaranteed for a period of 5 years. 
(iii) RITES should develop consultancy expertise outside Railway ai^ with 
a view to increase non-Railway consultancy business.

the Railways. 
(v) Inspection work related to quality assurance of purchased items, 
presently entrusted to RITES, may be handled by die Ministry of 
Railways. 
For disinvestment in IRCON International Ltd., recommendations of 
Disinvestment Commission are as under: 
(0 Strategic sale of 51% stake and transfer of management contgil in the 
company through a competitive bidding process, after having withdrawn 
necessary surplus from IRCON. 
(ii) With a view to ensuring the retention of the employees on deputation 
from Indian Railways as well as other key employees of IRCON, 
suitable schemes of incentivization of employees such as Employee 
Stock Option Plan (ESOP)/Employee Stock Purchase Scheme should 
be explored. 
(c) Ministry of Railways have not agreed to the recommendations and 
suggestions of Disinvestment Commission for disinvestments of RITES as 
listed in question (b) above for the following reasons: 
(i) the present net worth of RITES is Rs. 158 crores and the share capital 
is Rs. 2 crores for sale of 51% of shares to employees, the Government 
should be able to realise 51% of the net work i.e. Rs. 80 crores 
approximately. Thus the hundred rupee share would have to be sold 
for approximately Rs. 7800/-. Also the expected annual dividend of 
Rs. 3 crores, would yield an average return of only 1.9% to the 
employees. To realise Rs. 80 crores through employees as recommended 
156 

[29 November, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
by the Disinvestment Commission, on the average investment of the 
present employees of RITES, would be in the range of Rs. 3.5 lakhs 
per employee if all the present employees opt for it. This may not be 
possible. 
(i) deputation of Railway personnel to RITES, after disinvestments, would 
not be possible. 
(ii) Disinvestment Commission's suggestion that RITES may develop 
expertise in non-Railway business, after disinvestments, would defeat 
the very purpose for which RITES was initially set-up. Indian Railway's 
requirement of consultancy expertise in Railway area, would get 
diluted and may not be available after some time as availability of 
Railway expertise in RITES dwindles. 
(iv) the export of rolling stock was delegated to RITES only because 
Indian Railways was unable to handle it directly through Government 
departmental set up. The recommendations, if accepted, would 
immediately effect export of Railway rolling stock and Indian Railways' 
efforts to utilise spare capacity available in workshops. 
(v) the work of quality assurance for purchase items was hived off as a 
non-core activity to RITES as an independent third party. If Ministry 
of Railways were to carry out inspection work, they would need to 
create an organisation for the same at a time when Indian Railways are 
making every effort to contain growth of manpower. 
Ministry of Railways is not in favour of Disinvestment of IRCON 
International Ltd. due to following reasons: 
(0 IRCON is in the field of construction of Railway projects which are of 
specialised nature. 
(ii) Many of the projects undertaken abroad for construction and for 
operation of Railway system are given to the PSUs on the strength of 
Indian Railways backing, e.g. the Letter of Intent given by. the 
Malaysian Govt, for construction of US$ 1.5, billion Ipoh-Padang 
Besar doubling project on single tender without going through the 
process of formal tendering is only on the strength of the backing of 
Ministry of Railways, Government of India. 
(iii) Activities of IRCON abroad afford an oppontunity to Railway personnel 
to observe developments which benefit the Railway officers on 
repatriation- 
is? 

RAJYA SABHA [29 November, 2002} 
(iv) Indian Railways have got surplus manufacturing capacity in production 
units for manufacture of locomotives and coaches. IRCON is also the 
export arm of Indian Railways for the export of locomotives, coaches, 
etc. For export of locomotives and coaches, a close coordination 
between Railway Research Design and Standards Organisation, 
Indian Railways' manufacturing units and IRCON is required, 
(v) IRCON, being a construction organisation, can keep only a small work 
force on permanent basis. In the existing scenario of stiff competition 
in the construction industry, both in domestic and international market, 
only a company, which is lean with respect to their fixed cadre, can 
sustain their profits. Presently the skills,' for undertaking Rail related 
projects, are acquired by IRCON through personnel on deputation from 
the Railways. After disinvestments, it will not be possible to induct 
Railwaymen into IRCON. It will affect the competence of the 
organisation to carry out Rail related projects ' in India and abroad.

1190. SHRI RAJEEV SHUKLA: Will the Minister of YOUTH AFFAIRS AND 
SPORTS be pleased to state:

188 

[29 November, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) whether Government have made any provision for development of 
meritorious players at the national and international levels; and 
(d) if so, (he details thereof and the criteria being followed for providing 
financial assistance to such players? 
THE MRMISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF YOUTH AFFAIRS AND 
SPORTS (SHRI P. RADH A KRISHN AN): (a) Yes, Sir. From time to time proposals 
are received from the outstanding sportspersons of yesteryears living in indigent 
conditions for financial assistance 
(b) Yes, Sir. Under the following schemes. Government provides financial 
assistance to the outstanding/meritorious sportspersons:— 
(i) National Welfare Fund For Sportspersons: Under the scheme. 
Government gives monthly pensions upto Rs. 2500/- and one time 
lump-sum financial assistance upto Rs. 40.000/- for medical treatment 
to the retired sportspersons who have represented the country at 
national/international levels and living in indigent circumstances, i.e. 
whose monthly income is less than Rs. 3.000/- from all sources. 
(ii) Sports Fund for Meritorious Sports Persons: Under the scheme, 
meritorious sportspersons who have won medals in Olympic Games 
and Gold medal in World Cups/World Championships in Olympic and 
Asian Games disciplines are sanctioned monthly pensions @ Rs. 
2500/- Silver and Bronze medallists of World Cups/World 
Championships in Olympic and Asian Games disciplines and 
Commonwealth Games are sanctioned pension @ Rs. 2000/- per month. 
Pension is sanctioned from the age of 30 years for lifetime. 
(c) Yes, Sir.

level. Government provides Financial Assistance to the various National Sports 
Federations and Sportspersons under the following scheme: 
(i) Assistance to National Sports Federations: Under this scheme National 
Sports Federations are provided financial assistance for organization 
of National Coaching Camps, participation of athletes in International 
tournaments and engagement of foreign coaches and experts for 
meritorious sportspersons of National and International levels.

Under this scheme financial assistance upto Rs. 5 lakhs is sanctioned

undergoing training abroad, purchase of sports equipment, obtaining 
scientific support, and for training and participation in tournaments in 
the country. To get the assistance under the scheme, promising sports 
persons should not be more than 25 years of age. For sports like 
shooting, golf, billiards and snooker, chess and yachting the age limit 
may be relaxed upto 35 years. 
(iii) National Sports Development Funds:—Meritorious Sports persons 
seeking assistance under the scheme are also provided Financial 
Assistance for training.

NORTH KOREA 
SHR] RAJEEV SHUKLA (Uttar Pradesh): Madam, according to a recent 
newspaper column by a well-known journalist, a North Korean ship, carrying 
missile spares to Pakistan for its clandestine missile programme, was seized 
by the Coast Guard and Customs off Kandla Port in the summer of 2000. It 
was freed a few days later, after the captain pleaded that it was bound for Libya. 
The disquieting aspect is that Pakistan test-fired a few missiles, capable of 
carrying nuclear warheads, last month. By all accounts, it received the 
technology from North Korea. Notably, Pyongyang recently admitted to its 
nuclear capability, the technology for which, obviously, canie from Islamabad. 
It is a clear case of quid pro quo—Korea's missile technology for Pakistan's 
nuclear knowhow. It is apparent that the Korean ship's actual destination was 
Pakistan, and not Libya. 
Had the authorities acted with imagination, we could have prevented Pakistan 
from getting missile technology on the sly. It also highlights the need for toning up 
our intelligence agencies, including its external wing RAW, and better 
coordination between them and other authorities like the Coast Guard, the 
Customs and the Police. 
The Government should initiate a thorough probe into the whole episode and 
come out with a statement.

salaries. Therefore, this attitude, this work culture, has bejjn the major reason 
for our present day malaise. Suddenly we have got exposed to liberalisation, 
and here we have to compete with countries where the work culture is very 
different. People speak about China. More than 20 years back, China had 
introduced the policy of hire and fire, tf a person is not working properly, if he 
is not prone to discipline, he is thrown out, and nobody can do anything there. 
But, here, we are still battling as to how we rationalise the labour laws. The 
VRS schemes that have been offered are offering a fortune for a person to 
walk out. When I saw that I said, "How is it economical to throw him out at 
such a high cost". If that is the cost that is going lo be paid to get rid of one 
man who is not needed and who was recruited as a measure of gratis by a 
generous Minister, then where are we going to end up? So, the basis point is, 
we have to disinvest not the loss-making companies only. Who will buy the 
loss making companies? When it comes to that, they say that a particular 
company is making a tremendous profit. The BALCO was in the red. What 
happened to the BALCO since its disinvestment? The production went up 
several folds and it has now become an asset to the country. No matter who is 
running the industry. If it is generating wealth, it is generating wealth for the 
country. It does not matter who is running it. So, when the State is running a 
company, there is nobody responsible. That is because of our work culture. If 
it is disinvested, it starts yielding much higher returns for the investment that 
has been made therein. 
Sir, one point would be said as lo what should be done with the money that 
comes out of, this disinvestment process. There, I would like to suggest to the 
Government that that money should be kept aside for developmental projects, 
for infrastruclural development, for amelioration of the backward and the less 
fortunate people in the country. Those schemes should be financed from that. 
This money should not be utilised just for meeting the routine Government 
expenditure. That is not fair. When we are taking away money from a 
productive industry, we should invest in equally productive channels. That is the 
point the Government needs to address.

OBITUARY REFERENCE 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon. members, I refer with profound sorrow to the pass-
ing away of Shri Abu Abraham, a form er Member of the Rajya Sabha on the 
1" December, 2002 at the age of 78 years. 
Bom at Thiruvalla in Kerala in June, 1924, Shri Abu Abraham had his educa-
tion at the University College, Trivandrum. A journalist and cartoonist by pro-
fession, Shri Abraham was associated with several newspapers and journals. 
He started his career as a reporter of the Bombay Chronicle and later joined the 
Shankers' Weekly, New Delhi, in 1951. He was the only Indian cartoonist who 
worked in England for The Guardian and The Observer for 16 years as a political 
cartoonist. His cartoons earned him much popularity. He had many publications 
on cartoons to his credit. 
Shri Abu Abraham was a nominated Member of the Rajya Sabha from April. 
1972 to April, 1978. 
In the passing away of Shri Abu Abraham, the country has lost an eminent 
journalist and a noted cartoonist. 
We deeply mourn the passing away of Shri Abu Abraham. 
I request the Members to rise in thei r places and observe silence for one 
minute as a mark of respect to the memory of the departed soul. 
(Hon. Members then stood in silence for one minute.) 
MR. CHAIRMAN: The Secretary-General will convey to the members of the 
bereaved family our deep sense of sorrow and sympathy.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Expenditure on health care 
* 181. PROF. ALKA BALRAM KSHATRIYA: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that the expenditure on health care in 
percentage of GDP has been declining, whereas health care needs have grown j|^ 
steadily over the years; and ^ 
(b) the steps taken to raise the Central and State health outlays appropriately 
in view of the emerging new challenges to health and to ensure adequate health 
care facilities in all parts of the country? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI 
SHATRUGHAN SINHA): (a) and (b) A Statement is laid on the table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) As per World Health Report, 2002 of WHO, the percentage of total 
expenditure on health to GDP has remained in the vicinity of 5% since 1995. 
The health care needs over the years have no doubt grown with the increase in 
population, 
(b) Government has been making every ef fort to increase its contribution 
to public health expenditure. The resources for public investment in health 
sector are being augiTiented by securing assistance from various bilateral and 
multilateral agencies for implementation of various disease control 
programmes. To provide quality health care services to the people in the rural 
areas, especially the poor and the underserved, health infrastructure is being 
upgraded under the State Health Syst ems Project which is presently under 
implementation In seven States with World Bank assistance. The project will 
be gradually extended to other States. Additional Central Assistance is provided 
to States/UTs under the Prime Minister Gramodaya Yojana as well. 
The National Health Policy—2002 announced by the Government during 
the year envisages increasing public health investment to 2% of GDP by the 
year 2010 from the.existing 0.9%. It is also proposed in the Policy that State 
Governments would increase their expenditure on health sectors to 7% of their 
total budget by 2005 and to 8% of the budget by 2010. The Central 
Government contribution would rise to 25% from the existing 15% by 2010. 
Government is making all efforts to increase expenditure on health as per the 
Policy subject to overall financial constraints, The Tenth Plan outlay for Central 
Health Sector subject to approval (by National Development Council) has been 
fixed at Rs. 9253 crore compared to Rs. 5118 crore during the Ninth Plan.

WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) the estimated number of AIDS/HIV positive women and men in the age

THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI 
SHATRUGHAN SfNH A): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the table of the House. 
Statement 
The National AIDS Control Organization, Government of India conducts 
Nation wide HIV Sentinel Surveillance every year during the period August-
October, covering both high-risk groups as well as general population. This 
data is also used to estimate the burden of HIV infections in the country in the 
adult population between 15-49 years of age group by taking certain assump-

tions into consideration. However, disaggregated HIV estimates in various age 
groups are not made. Based on the HIV Sentinel Surveillance data from 1999, 
estimate of 3.7 million HIV infections was made, which include 2.2 million 
i n f e c t i o n s  a m o n g  m e n  a n d   1 . 5  million i n f e c t i o n s  a m o n g  w o m e n .  
The estimated number of HIV infections in the year 1998 was 3.5 million, 
1999 as 3.7 million, 2000 as 3.86 million and 2001 as 3.97 million infections. 
These estimates indicate that there has not been much upsurge in the spread 
of HIV infection in the country. 
As per reports received from States/UTs in the country, 1372 AIDS deaths 
have been reported to National AIDS Control Organisation during last three 
years. A Statement (Statement-I) indica ting number of deaths State-wise and 
year-wise during each of last three years is annexed. (See below). 
Government of India is implementing a Nation-wide comprehensive National 
AIDS Control Programme through autonomous AIDS Control Societies at State, 
UT and Municipal levels. The main components of the programme are:- 
(i) Reducing the HIV transmission amongst poor and marginalized sec-
tions of the community at the high risk of infection, by (a) targeted 
interventions amongst marginalized sections of the society at the h igh-
est risk of HIV infection and transmission such as sex workers, trans-
port work TS, injecting drug users, men who have sex with men, m igrant 
workers, industrial workers vulnerable to HIV infection, street children 
and slum population; (b) control of sexually transmitted diseases 
through syndromic management at the peripheral public health institu-
tions and through outreach services; and (c) condom promotion to 
prevent the sexual transmission of HIV; 
(ii) Reducing the spread of HIV amongst general population, which is 
perceived to be at a lower risk; by (a) reducing blood based transmis-
sion by modernizing the blood transfusion services in the country for 
greater availability and rational use of blood, by ensuring mandatory 
screening of HIV, Hepatitis 'B' and 'C, malaria and syphilis and by 
developing technical manpower; (b) Information, Education and Com-
munication campaigns to raise awareness levels; and (c) promotion of 
voluntary counseling and testing for HIV; 
(iii) Strengthen the institutions responsible for implementation of the 
programme, by—(a) increasing the quantity, quality and timeliness 
of surveillance systems for HIV, sexually transmitted infections, 
behaviour patterns and social determinants in all parts of the country

technical and managerial capacities of State AIDS Control Societies

rational Research & Development; 
(iv) Delivery of community based low cost care for people living with 
HIV/AIDS, by—(a) providing drugs for treatment of opportunistic 
infections includingTuberculosis;(b)antiretroviral post exposure pro-

(v) Ensuring multisectoral collaboration with public, private and voluntary

700 targeted intervention projects in the country are being run through

programme.

Statement 
The measures adpoted to control population by the Government have yielded 
favourable results, the Total Fertility Rate has come down from 6in 1951 to3.2 
in 1999. The Birth Rate has come down from 40.8 in 1951 to 25.8 during the year 
2000. as per the estimates of Sample Registration System (SRS), Registrar General 
of India. According to National Family Health Survey conducted in 1998-99, 
42% ofthe couples with two children and about 58% of couples with 3 children 
have adopted terminal methods of contraception. The child population (0—6 
yeai^) has come down from 18% in 1991 to 15% in 2001 census, showing decline 
in fertility rate. 
Among the major States with more than 20 million population, the States of 
Kerala and Tamil Nadu have already achieved a replacement level of fertility of a 
TFR of 2.1, while the States of Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat. Karnataka, Maharashtra, 
Orissa, Punjab and West Bengal are having a TFR of 2.2 to 3.0 and are in the 
direction ofreplacement level of fertility. There are 4 States v/r. Assam, Madhya 
Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and Haryana which are having a TFR of 3.1 to 4.0, while 
the 4 States of Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and Jharkhand have recorded a 
TFR of 4.1 to 4.7 as per the SRS, 1999.

with two children have high acceptance in Southern and Western regipns, being

(a) and (b) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) As per sectoral poJicy on FDI in telecom Sector, caps applicable 
to foreign equity participation under different activities are as under: 
1. In basic and cellular telephony, FDI is permitted up to 49%. 
2. No equity cap is applicable to manufacturing activities. 
1 In the following activities of the telecom sector, FDI up to 100% is 
allowed, subject to divestment of 26% equity in favour of Indian 
public within a period of 5 years, if listed elsewhere: 
a) ISPs not providing gateways (both for satellite and submarine

c) Electronic Mail; and 
d) Voice Mail.

of Ministers (GoM) on FDI, to deci de necessary changes. The Steering 
Committee on FDI, which was set up by the Planning Commission has, inter 
alia, recommended enhancement of the FDI cap in respect of basic and cellular 
telephony to 74% (from 49%) and in total bandwidth and gateway to 100%

Steps to assist the ailing tea industry 
1197. SHRI KARNENDU BHATTACHARJEE: Will the Minister of 
COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the news-item 
captioned "Darjeeling in Act will help Tea Industry", which appeared in the 
Asian Age, dated the 10th October, 2002; 
(b) if so, Government's reaction thereto; and 
(c) the steps proposed to address the problem highlighted in the news-
item, so as to assist the ailing Tea Indu stry to compete with neighbouring tea 
producing countries like Sri Lanka and Nepal? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI RAJIV PRATAP RUDI): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. The Government 
has initiated action to protect Darjeeling tea under various legal frameworks 
that exist in different importing countries. The Darjeeling tea logo is registered 
in various countries including UK, Germany, Italy, Switzerland, Belgium, 
Netherlands, Portugal, USA, Japan, Egypt and Canada. The Darjeeling tea 
word and logo are registered as a Certification Trade Mark in India and would 
also be registered under the Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration 
and Protection) Act 1999, once it is operationalised. 
(c) While Sri Lankan tea is not similar in character to Darjeeling tea and 
hence does not pose a direct competition vis-a-vis the requirements of the 
Darjeeling tea in export markets, Nepal tea poses a competitive challenge to 
Darjeeling tea. The agro-climauc condition, under which Nepal teas are grown, 
is closer to that of Darjeeling with the added advantage of newer bushes. 
Darjeeling tea, however, has greater brand value and image and the Government 
has taken action to protect the brand name legally as well as implement a 
monitoring system that will address the problem of alleged misuse.

Relief package to coffee growers 
1199. SHRI PRASANTA CHATTERJEE: Will the Minister of COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government propose to liberalise the credit package i.e. Liberal 
Export Credit, higher moratorium period and simpler norms for fresh loans for 
the Coffee growers; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether this would help to provide relief to the beleaguered Coffee plan-
tation; and 
(d) the steps taken to monitor the situation for implementation of the pack-
age? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI RAJIV PRATAP RUDI): (a) and (b) Concerned with the prob-
lems of the coffee growers, who are facing hardships due to prevailing low 
prices, the Government of India have taken a series of steps in the recent 
months for the benefit of the coffee sector. This includes a special relief pack-
age for the coffee growers (announced by the Reserve Bank of India) under 
which the term loans as well as crop loans of the Banks have been consolidated 
into a Special Coffee Term Loan (SCTL) with repayment period of 9-11 years 
and repayment holiday of 3 years. The package includes grant of fresh loans, 
reduction of interest rate on SCTL by 1 %, deferment of interest due on SCTL 
during the current year to be recovered over the next 3 years etc. In addition, 
the Government of India is also providing 5% interest relief to small growers on 
the working capital loans taken by them from financial institutions, besides a 
package of incentives for export of coffee and implementing innovative market-
ing strategies in the international as well as domestic markets to arrest the 
decline in exports and also to increase domestic consumption etc. Further, the 
Tenth Five Year Plan programmes and schemes of the Coffee board have been 
formulated to ensure long-term devel opment of the sector. Recently, on the 
advice of the Government, the National Bank for Agricultural and Rural Devel-
opment (NABARDJ has also set up a "Plantation Industry Cell", for providing 
prompt attention to the credit related problems of the plantation industry. 
As regards liberal export credit, the general concessions available to the 
exporters such as availab ility of credit at concessional rate of interest from 
bsnks in respect of pre-shipment and post-shipment advances to exporters are 
available to coffee exporters also. 
57 

RAJYA SABHA [2 December, 2002] 
(c) The implementation of above measures particularly SCTL package will 
effectively postpone the repayment of debt, provide for need based fresh crop 
loans after rescheduling the existing crop loans and result in reduced cost of 
loans. All these measures will provide reliefto the coffee growers. 
(d) The Government of India has been continuously monitoring/reviewing 
the implementation of the SCTL package. The banks and Coffee Board through 
their extension network have also been disseminating the information regard-
ing relief packages to the coffee growers for successful implementation of the 
package.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) and (b ) The recent repon of the National 
Intelligence Council (NIC) states that the number of people with HIV/AIDS 
will grow significantly by the end of the decade. The increase will be driven 
by the spread of the disease in five populous countries: Nigeria. Ethiopia. 
Russia, India and China, where the number of infected people will grow from 
around 14 to 23 million currently to an estimated 50 to 75 million by 2010. 
It is reported that the HIV/AIDS is spreading at different rates in the five 
countries, with the epidemic being most advanced in Nigeria and Ethiopia. 
The official adult prevalence rate is al most 6 per cent in Nigeria, between 10 
and 18 per cent in Ethiopia, around I to 2 per cent in Russia, around I per cent 
in India and 0.15 to 0.25 per cent in China. Heterosexual transmission of the 
HIV virus is the primary mode to spread In Nigeria, Ethiopia and India- 
while Intravenous drug use drives the spread of the disease in Russia. Several 
factors are driving the epidemic in China — the large migrant population, 
Intravenous drug users and poor hygiene in plasma sales. 
The National AIDS Control Organisation, Government of India conducts 
Nation wide HIV Sentinel Surveillance every year during the period 
August—October. This data is also used to estimate the burden of HIV 
infections in the country in the adults population between 15— 49 years of 
age group by taking certain assumptions into consideration. Based on the HIV 
Sentinel Surveillance data from 2001, estimate of 3.9? million HIV infections 
was made. As such, Government does not agree with the NIC (National 
Intelligence Council) report. 
(c) 1372 deaths due to AIDS have been reported to National AIDS Control 
Organisation during last three years. Based on annual round of HIV Sentinel 
surveillance 2001, it is estimated that th ere are 3.97 million HIV infections in 
the country.

(d) The Government of India is implementing Second Phase of the National 
AIDS Control Programme which has two key objectives: 
(1) To reduce the spread of HIV infection in India; and (2) to strengthen 
India's capacity to respond to HIV/AIDS on a long term basis. 
The programme has five distinct components with specific strategies under 
each of them. 
(i) Reducing the HIV transmission amongst poor and marginalized 
sections of the community at the high risk of infection, by (a) 
targeted interventions amongst marginalized sections of the society 
at the highest risk of HIV infection and transmission such as sex 
workers, transport workers, injecting drug users, men who have 
sex with men, migrant workers, industrial workers vulnerable to 
HIV infection, street children, slum population; (b) control of 
sexually diseases through syndromic management at the peripheral 
public health institutions and through outreach services; and (c) 
condom promotion to prevent the sextual transmission of HIV; 
(ii) Reducing the spread of HIV amongst general population, which is 
perceived to be at a lower risk; by (a) reducing blood based 
transmission by modernizing the blood transfusion services in the 
country for greater availability and rational use of blood, by 
ensuing mandatory screening of HIV, Hepatitis 'B' and 'C, malaria 
and syphilis and by developing technical manpower; (b) 
Information, education and Communication campaigns to raise 
awareness levels; and (c) promotion of voluntary counselling and 
testing for HIV; 
(iii) Strengthen the institutions responsible for implemention of the 
programme, by — (a) increasing the quantity, quality and timeliness 
of surveillance systems for HIV, sexually transmitted infections, 
behaviour patterns and social determinants in all parts of the 
country so as to enable evidence based planning and response; 
(b) improving technical and manage rial capacity of State AIDS 
Control Societies for the effective implementation of the programme; 
(c) training of medical and para-medical personnel in management 
of HIV/AIDS patients; and (d) supporting high level peer reviewed 
competitive and rational Research and Development; 
(iv) delivery of community based low cost care for people living with 
HIV/AIDS, by — (a) providing drugs for treatment of opportunistic

by the New Drug division in the office of DCG (1). The requirement for granting 
such approvals are specified in Rules 122Ato 122E and Schedule Y of Drugs and 
Cosmetics Act and Rules made thereunder. 
The evaluation of new drug applications is a complex process as per 
Schedule-V under Drugs and Cosmetics rules and varies according to the 
nature of molecule/drug, published data and information furnished by the

take on an average 3 to 5 years for an applicant to complete all phase of trials

tested on human being anywhere in th e world); about 1—3 years for the first 
time approval of the drug already approved elsewhere but requiring confirma-
tory clinical trial, and about 2-3 months for subsequent applications for al-
ready approved drugs. This is however, subject to submission of all required 
data as per provisions of Schedule-Y of Drug and Cosmetics Rules and opin-

suppresent, etc., which are critical from the point of view of public health are 
cleared on a fast track basis.

ILY WELFARE be pleased to state:

sections of the society from AIDS infection under the said policy; and 
(c) the places in backward and trib al areas of Andhra Pradesh where 
voluntary test facilities of HIV infections are set-up/proposed to be set-up in 
accordance with the said policy? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) to (c) The salient features of National AIDS 
Prevention and Control Policy are as under;— 
(i) to prevent the epidemic from sp reading further and to reduce the im-
pact of the epidemic not only upon the infected persons but upon the 
health and socio-economic status of the general population at all 
levels. 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
97 

RAJYA SABHA [2 December, 2002] 
(ii) to reiterate strongly the Government's firm comm itment to prevent the 
spread of HIV infection and reduce personal and social impact, 
(iii) to generate a feeling of ownership among all the participants both at 
the Government and non-Government levels, like the Central Minis-
tries and agencies of the Government of india. State Governments, city 
corporations, industrial undertakings in public and private sectors, 
panchayat institutions and local bodies to make it a truly national 
efforts, 
(iv) to create an enabling socio-economicf'environment for prevention of 
HIV/AIDS, to provide care and support to people living with HIV/ 
AIDS and to ensure protection/promotion of their human rights 
including right to access health car e system, right to education, 
employment and privacy, to mobilise support of a large number of 
NGOs/Community Based Organisations (CBOs) for an enlarged 
community initiative for prevention and alleviation of the HIV/AIDS 
problem, 
(v) to decentralise HIV/AIDS control programme to the field level with 
adequate financial and administrative delegation of responsibilities, 
(vi) to strengthen programme management capabilities at the State 
Governments, municipal corporations, panchayat institutions and lead-
ing NGOs participating in the programme, 
(vii) to bring in horizonta! integration at the implementation level with other 
national programmes like Reproductive and Child Health, TB Control, 
Integrated Child Development Scheme and with the primary health care 
system, 
(viii) to prevent women, children and other socially weak groups from 
becoming vulnerable to HIV infection by improving health education, 
legal status and economic prospects,

Adequate voluntary testing facilities with pre-test and post-test coun-
selling should be made available throughout the country in a phased 
manner. There should be at least one HIV testing centre in each district 
in the country with proper counselling facilities, 
(x) to provide adequate and equitabl e provision of health care to HIV-
infected people and to draw attention to the compelling public health

rationale for overcoming stigmatisation, discrimination and seclusion 
in society,

port and cooperation in the field of research in vaccines, drugs, emerg-

(xii) to ensure availability of adequate and safe blood and blood products 
for the genera! population through promotion of voluntary blood do-
nation in the country, and

cially students, youth and other sexually active sections to generate

National Testing Policy on HIV 
1275. DR. C. NARAYANA REDDY: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether there are any regulations to monitor the implementation of the 
norms of National Testing Policy on HIV; 
123 

RAJYA SABHA [2 December, 2002] 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the provisions to check flouting of the norms? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) to (c) Government of India has approved the 
National AIDS Prevention and Control Policy in April, 2002 which clearly 
states that there is no public health rational for mandatory testing of a person 
for HIV/AIDS. HIV testing should be carried out on a voluntary basis with 
appropriate pre-test and post-test counselling. These guidelines have been 
circulated to all State Governments for implementation. The statement in this 
regard is given below: 
Statement 
The details and the provisions to check flouting of the norms are in the "para 
5.6" of "National AIDS Prevention and Control Policy" 
"5.6 my testing 
5.6.1 There is an active debate in the country on the issue of mandatory 
testing of people suspected of carrying HIV infection. Considerable thought 
has been given to this issue. The Government feels that there is no public 
health rationale for mandatory testing of a person for HIV/AIDS. On the other 
hand, such an approach could be coun ter-productive as it  may scare away a 
large number of suspected cases from getting detected and treated. HIV testing 
carried out on a voluntary basis with appropriate pre-test and post-test 
counselling is considered to be a better strategy and is in line with the WHO 
guidelines on HIV testing. Government of India has earlier issued a comprehensive 
HIV testing policy and the following issues are reiterated here:- 
(I) No individual should be made to undergo a mandatory testing for HIV. 
(ii) No mandatory HIV testing shoul d be imposed as a precondition for 
employment or for providing health care facilities during employment. 
However, in the case of Armed Forces, before employment, HIV 
screening may be carried out voluntarily with pretest and post-test 
counselling and the results may be kept confidential. 
(iii) Adequate voluntary testing fac ilities with pre-test and post-test 
counselling should be made available throughout the country in a 
phased manner. There should be at least one HIV testing centre in 
each district in the country with proper counselling facilities. 
(iv) In case a person likes to get the HIV status verified through testing, all 
necessary facilities should be given to that person and results 
124 

[2 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
should be kept strictly confidential. Such results should be given out 
to the person and with his consent to the members of his family. 
Disclosure of the HIV status to the spouse or sexual partner of the 
person should invariably be done by the attending physician with 
proper counselling. However, the person should also be encouraged 
to share this information with the family for getting proper home-
based care and emotional support from the family members. 
(v) In case of marriage, if one of the pa rtners insists on a test to check the 
HIV status of the other partner; such tests should be carried out by the 
contracting party to the satisfaction of the person concerned. 
5.6.2. The HIV testing policy adopted is found to be appropriate for different 
types of testing done under the programme. At present people are tested for- 
(a) Screening in blood banks 
(b) epidemiological surveys; and 
(c) confirmatory testing for clinical management and voluntary testing. 
In the case of screening for blood donation, a single test of ERS (ELISA/ 
Rapid/Simple) is conducted to eliminate HIV sero-reactive blood. In the case 
of epidemiological surveys, two tests either with ELISA, or Rapid or Simple 
will be done. In both these cases the testing is unlinked and anonymous. In 
the case of diagnosis of clinically su spected cases and for voluntary testing, 
the testing will be done with 3 ERS us ing HIV kits with different antigens. 
HIV testing under these conditions will be carried out with proper pre-testing 
and post-testing counselling with informed consent of the individual and with 
proper follow up facilities. 
5.6.3 in case of HIV testing facilities in the private sector hospitals, clinics, 
nursing homes and diagnostic centres, the State Governments should adopt 
legislative and other measures to ensure  that these testing centres conform to 
the national policy and guidelines relating to HIV testing."

THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING (SHRMATI 
SUSHMA SWARAJ): (a) Yes Sir. 
(b) to (d) Under the Industrial Bank of India (IDBI) Act, 1964 Section 2(c) (xvii) 
"Entertainment Industry including films" has been included as an 'approved 
activity' under 'industrial concern'. Both IDBI as well as RBI have formulated 
schemes/guidelines specifically for financing production of films by financial 
institutions and public sector banks respectively. 
As per RBI guidelines, Public Sector Banks may finance production of films 
of producers with good track record subject to certain conditions. The RBI 
guidelines state that ordinarily producers are required to bring in at least 25 per 
cent of the project cost as promoters contribution and also tie up with the 
distributors and receive advances as per usual practices to cover 35 per cent to 
40 per cent of the budget. It has thus been stipulated in the guidelines that bank 
advances would be for the balance requirement of 35 to 40 per cent of the cost. 
However, in deserving cases where the Banks are quite comfortable with the 
project as well as the background of the producers, the financing can be in-
creased upto 50 per cent of the project cost on merits. 
Under IDBI's scheme financial institutions are to initially focus on financing 
film production activity of corporate entities. While there is no upper hmit for 
sanction, the minimum quantum of assistance would normally be not less than

rights etc. The period of repayment of loan would not exceed two years and 
loans would be sanctioned against various forms of securities specified in the 
scheme.

modes of dispute resolution including conciliation, emdiation and arbitration.

have been set up to expedite the disposal of cases. Information technology is

Adoption of Court Management Techniques 
1306. SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIRI GIREDDY: Will the Minister of 
LAW AND JUSTICE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are laying emphasis on adoption of Court 
Management techniques by the subordinate courts for reducing the huge 
backlog of pending cases; and 
(b) if so, the details of the Court Management techniques? 
THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI K. JANA 
KRISHNAMURTHY): (a) and (b) The su bordinate Judiciary is under the 
control of the concerned High Courts. It is primary responsibility of the High 
Courts to take necessary action regarding Court Management in consultation 
with the respective State Governments.  However the Supreme Court of India 
has taken a number of measures to redu ce the pendency in the Supreme Court 
which, inter-alia, include the following:— 
(i)   More practical categorization & grouping of cases 
(ii)   Stabilization of Benches 
(iii) As far as possible cases scheduled to be taken up for hearing on a day 
should be listed for that day. 
(iv) No accumulation of defective matters. 
(v) Reservation of more and sufficient slots for old pending Misc. and SLP 
matters, so that they are listed in  chronological order in sufficient 
numbers. 
166

(vi) Better utilization of available computer network. 
(vil) Streamlining of administration and manpower so that there is neither 
excess nor less work at every desk, and to make constant efforts for 
improving the quality of work by the Registry staff. 
High Courts have been requested to adopt similar measures to reduce the 
pendency of cases. The High Courts have also been requested to implement 
the recommendations of the Malimath Committee to streamline procedure 
which will, inter-alia, expedite disposal of pending cases. 
The Central Government has initiated a pilot project for Computerisation 
of City Civil Courts in the four metropolises of Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and

An amount of Rs. 518.76 lakhs has been released during 2002-2003 for

Centrally Sponsored Scheme. This will include establishment of computerised 
enquiry/facilitation centres in the high Courts.

Statement 
Extracts taken from guidelines For drinking water quality (Second 
Edition), Volume I Recommendations, World Health Organisation, 
Geneva 1993. 
Iron 
Iron is one of the most abundant metals in the earth's crust. It is found in 
natural fresh waters at levels ranging from 0.5 to 50 mg/litre. Iron may also be 
present in drinking water as a result of the use of iron coagulants or the 
corrosion of steel and cast iron pipes during water distribution. 
Iron Is an essential element in human nutrition. Estimates of minimum 
daily requirement for iron depend on age, sex, physiological status, and iron 
bio-availability and range from about 10 to 50 mg/day. 
As a precaution-against storage in the body of excessive iron, in 1983, 
JECFA established a provisional maximum tolerable daily intake (PMTDI) of 
0.8 mg/kg. of body weight, which applies to iron from all sources except for 
iron oxides used as colouring agents, and iron supplements taken during 
pregnancy and lactation or for specific clinical requirements. An allocation of 
10% of this PMTDI to drinking water gives a value of about 2 mg/litre which 
does not present a hazard to health. The taste and appearance of drinking 
water will usually be affected below this level. 
Anaerobic ground water may contain ferrous iron at concentration of upto 
several milligrams per litre without discoloration or turbidity in water when 
directly pumped from a well. On exposure to the atmosphere, however, the 
ferrous iron oxidizes to ferric iron, giving an objectionable reddish-brown 
colour to the water. 
Iron also promotes the growth of "iron bacteria", which derive their energy 
from the oxidation of ferrous iron to ferriq iron and in the process deposit a 
slimy coating on the piping. 
At levels above 0.3 mg/litre. iron stains laundry and plumbing fixtures. 
There is usually no noticeable taste at iron concentrations below 0.3 mg/litre 
although turbidity and colour may develop. Iron concentrations of I—3 mg/ 
litre can be acceptable for people drinking anaerobic well-water. 
No health-based guideline value is proposed for iron.

Implementation of Delhi Rent Control Act, 1995 
1338. SHRI DWIJENDRA NATH SHARMAH: Will the Minister of URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) the steps Government have, so far, taken in the implementation/ 
enforcement of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1995; 
(b) the reasons for the delay and by when it is likely to be notified; 
(c) the details of the recommendations of the Parliamentary Standing 
Committee on Delhi Rent Control (A mendment) Bill, 1997, accepted by 
Government; and 
(d) by when these are likely to be implemented/notified? 
196 

[2 December. 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MFNISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN DEVELOPMENT 
AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI O. RAJAGOPAL): (a) and (b) The Delhi 
Rent Act, 1995 was enacted in 1995. The Act has, however, not come into 
force so far primarily because, soon af ter the Delhi Rent Bill was passed by 
the Parliament, a section of tenants, pa rticularly the trader-tenants launched 
an agitation against the Bill and demanded changes in some of the provisions 
of the Bill. The matter was examined by the Government and in June, 1997 it 
was decided to carry out amendments in the Delhi Rent Act, 1995 before 
bringing it into force. Accordingly, the Delhi Rent (Amendment) Bill, 1997 was 
introduced in the Rajya Sabha on 28.7.1997. The Bill was then referred to the 
Parliamentary Standing Committee on Urban and Rural Development to examine 
and report. The Committee presented Its report on the Delhi Rent (Amendment) 
Bill, 1997 to the Lok Sabha on 21.12.2000 and also laid it on the Table of the 
Rajya Sabha on the same day i.e. 21.12.2000. 
(c) and (d) Broadly the recommendations are: 
(i) The monthly rental limit be increased from Rs. 3500/- to Rs. 7500/-
for the purpose of applicability of the Act. 
(ii) The format and procedure for rent agreement be prescribed. 
(iii) The period of inheritability in respect of tenancies of non-residential 
premises be increased from three years to five years. 
The Government considered the Report of the Committee and accepted all 
its recommendations.. A notice for movi ng official amendments to the 
Amendment Bill has also been given to the Secretary-General. Rajya Sabha. 
At present the Bitl is pending before the Rajya Sabha for its consideration. 
After the Bill is passed by the Parliament  and assented to by the President, 
action will be taken to bring the Delhi Rent Act, 1995 along with amendments 
into force.

AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI O. RAJAGOPAL): (a) The said machines

utilization of these machines is 4.67%. The audit has assessed this capacity 
utilization on the basis of rated capacity. The audit has multiplied the maximum 
speed of the machine with the total annual working hours. In reply to these 
observations of audit, it has been explained that capacity utilization is worked

speed can only be achieved in Ideal conditions which do not exist in practice.

the nature of jobs and various other fact ors. With the passage of time there is 
erosion in the operational efficiency of the machine also. Therefore, the 
Annual Assessed Capacity of the machine is assessed at regular intervals and 
it keeps on changing with passage of time. This clarification had been provided 
to the audit on 7.8.2001 and no further comments have so far been received 
frqm the audit. The capacity utilization on the basis of assessed capacity is

SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE (West Bengal):   Madam, I move: 
"That this House disapproves the Delhi Metro Railway (Operation 
and Maintenance) Ordinance, 2002 (No. 7 of 2002)) promulgated

Madam, Deputy Chairperson, at the very outset, I would like to 
make it quite clear that we are not obstructing, or, we are not going to 
reject this Bill by disapproving it. But, we want to register our protest 
because this Legislation has been brought through the Ordinance route. 
Madam, you are fully aware tbat under Ar ticle 123 of the Constitution, the 
President or the Executive is ve sted with the power to promulgate 
Ordinances during the recess period of Parliament. What is the basic 
objective of this power given to the Executive? The basic objective is to 
ensure that the work of the Executive does not come to a standstill, when 
Parliament is not in Session. Therefore, during the interregnum period, the 
Executive  is  vested  with  law-making  authority. Otherwise,  it  is the 
exclusive domain of the Parliament to make laws. But certain exigencies might 
arise during the interregnum period, that is, when Parliament is not in Session. 
At that time, the Executive, can exercise its Ordinance-making authority.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
NPAs of State Finance Corporation 
*201. DR. ABRAR AHMED: 
SHRI RAJEEV SHUKLA: 
Will the Minister of FINANCE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a large number of State Finance Corporations are 
very sick and burdened with a large amount of Non-Performing Assets; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) in what manner Government proposes to rehabilitate the State Finance 
Corporations and deal with their large Non-Performing Assets? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI 
JASWANT SINGH); (a) to (c) A Statement is placed on the Table -f the House. 
Statement 
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Out of the 18 State Finance Corporations (SFCs) four, that is of, Delhi, 
Kerala, Rajasthan and West Bengal have a positive net worth as on 31 st March. 
2002. The net worth, however, of the remaining 14 SFCs stands fully eroded. 
The accumulated losses of all these SFCs, during 2001-02, aggregates to Rs. 
4,198 crores. NPAs of SFCs as a whole were 61% of the loans and advances, 
as at the end of Marcn 2002.1 he amount involved is Rs. 7076 crores. 
Standard Assets constitute only 39%. 

RAJYA SABHA [3 December, 2002] 
(c) The SFCs Act was amended in 2000 for providing flexibility and 
functional autonomy to them. A Committee headed by Shri G.P. Gupta, the 
then CMD, IDBI looked into their functioning and submitted a report 
recommending, inter-alia, financial, operational and organisational re-
structuring of SFCs. The report of th e Committee has been sent to various 
SFCs for taking immediate action on recommendations that do not involve any 
financial support, such as operational a nd organisational restructuring. SFCs 
being State entities, the State Governme nts are the principal stakeholders. 
They are thus expected to consider steps for improving the performance and 
recapitalisation of SFCs. In order to attract long term refinance from Financial 
Institutions, SFCs have to improve recovery of NPAs and reestablish their 
viability.

Exploration of oil and natural gas in Krishna-Godawari basin 
*202. DR. DASARI NARAYANA RAO: Will the Minister of PETRO-
LEUM AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) what is the present status of exploration of oil and natural gas in 
Krishna-Godawari basin in Andhra Pradesh by ONGC; 
(b) whether any headway has been achieved in finding oil and gas reserves 
in the basin; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS {SHRI RAM 
NAIK): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table. 
Statement 
(a) to (c) Besides acquiring 32,574 Ground Line Kms. (GLK) of 2D and 
19,799 GLK of 3D of seismic data, Oil and Natural Gas Corporation Ltd. 
(ONGC) has drilled 323 exploratory and 27 development wells in Krishna-
Godavari (KG) onland basin in the State of Andhra Pradesh as on 
01.10.2002.These exploratory efforts of ONGC in Andhra Pradesh have led to 
the discovery of 41 hydrocarbon finds, of which 8 are oil and gas finds and 33 
are gas finds. Further, as on 01.04.2002, from these finds ONGC has 
established 56.5 Million Metric Tonnes (MMT) ultimate reserves of oil and 
oil equivalent gas (O+OEG), of which 51.7 Billion Cubic Metres (BCM) are 
ultimate gas reserves. 
In addition to the above onland areas, ONGC has acquired 46,650

Line Kms. (LKM) of 2D and 81,819 LKM of 3D seismic data and has drilled 
104 exploratory wells in KG offshore. The exploration efforts by ONGC in 
these offshore areas have resulted in 8 hydrocarbon finds, of which 4 are oil 
and gas finds and 4 are gas finds. As on 01.04.2002, ONGC has establi.shed 
from these finds, 9.3 MMT of ultimate reserves of 0+OEG, of which 6.5 BCM 
are ultimate gas reserves. Further, in 1980s ONGC had made 2 more

was relinquished by ONGC being non-commercial and Ravva field in

participating interest.

SHRI RAM NAIK: Madam, as far as time-bound programme is concerned, 
I would say that every block is allott ed to a party. The awardee, while 
submitting its bid, gives their phase-wise programme. The committee, headed 
by the Director-General of Hydrocarbons, look into the Issue whether it is 
going as per schedule. As far as allotment of blocks under NELP 1, 2 and 3 
and so far as exploration in Krishna-Godavari Basin is concerned, It is going 
as per the schedule. 
The second paft of the supplementary put by the hon. Member is whether 
any gas is earmarked for Andhra Pradesh. According to the New Exploration 
Licensing Policy, the awardee is free to sell it on commercial basis at 
commercial rates. So, as such, there is no directive from the Government of 
India. But, since the gas has been found in Andhra Pradesh, naturally, the oil would 
be cheaper in Andhra Pradesh. I see a picture that the way Gujarat has been 
benefited by having gas reserves in Gujarat and in the western shore, the 
maximum beneficiary, in this case, would be Andhra Pradesh.

*217. SHRI RUMANDLA RAMACHANDRAIAH : Will the Minister of

ern rivers was found technically feasible in a study by National Water

into the sea; and

38

THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES {SHRI ARJUN CHARAN 
SETHI) : (a) to (d) tn 1980, the Ministry of Water Resources, then known as 
the Ministry of Irrigation, formulated a National Perspective Plan for 
integrated water resources development through inter-linkages of several 
southern-based Peninsular rivers and the Himalayan rivers. The Government 
of India established the National Water Development Agency (NWDA) in 
1982 as an autonomous society to ca rryout water balance and feasibility 
studies of the Peninsular and Himalayan rivers. The -Peninsular Component 
of the National Perspective Plan envisages inter-llnking of Mahanadi-
Godavari-Krishna-Pennar-Cauvery-Vaigai. As per the water balance studies 
of various river basins of the penins ular Component conducted by National 
Water Development Agency, Mahanadi and Godavari river basins are surplus 
in water, whereas the river basins namely. Krishna, Pennar, Cauvery and 
Vaigai are deficit. It is. therefore, pr oposed to transfer the surplus water of 
Mahanadi which in turn will be receiving water from the Himalayan 
component and Godavari basins to Krishna basin by inter-linking Mahanadi 
to Godavari and Godavari to Krishna.  The water, thus received in Krishna 
basin is proposed to be transferred to Pennar, Cauvery and Vaigai basins. 
NWDA has identified 9 links under this part of the Peninsular Component for 
preparation of feasibility report and has prepared f easibility reports for three 
links. Implementation of the water transfer links would only be possible if the 
concerned co-basin States agree to the water linkage proposal and provide 
other logistical support necessary for project implementation and availability 
of fund is ensured.

Features of the Special VRS for the employees declared surplus 
(a) All permanent employees rendered surplus irrespective of their age and 
qualifying service can opt for the scheme.

amount equal to basic pay plus dearness allowance for the number of days 
worked out on the basis of length of service @ 35 days for each completed 
year and 25 days for each remaining year. For any part of a year, the number of 
days, for ex-gratia-amount, will be worked out on the basis of 365 days in a 
year. The ex-gratia amount will be further subject to the following conditions : 
(i)    Total number of years to be counted for payment of ex-gratia will 
not exceed 33 years;

of calculation of ex-gratia; 
(iii) The ex-gratia will be subject to a minimum of Rs. 25,000/- or 250 
days emoluments, whichever is higher; 
(iv) The ex-gratia amount should not exceed the sum of the basic pay 
plus DA that the employee would draw at the prevailing level for 
the balance of the period of service left before superannuation; 
(v)    The ex-gratia amount will be paid in lump sum; 
(vi) The ex-gratia amount up to Rs. 5.00 lakhs will be exempted from 
Income Tax;

given under CCS (Pension) Rules, 1972 to such permanent surplus 
employees who have rendered a minimum of 15 years of qualifying

Guidelines for foreign Banks 
1421. SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA: Will the Minister of FINANCE 
AND COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether there are any guidelines i ssued by the Reserve Bank of India 
to regulate the functioning of foreign Banks in India; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether the RBI exercises any effective control on these foreign Banks 
and if so, in what manner; 
(d) whether the foreign banks are permitted to close down their business in 
India at any time without due notice to concerned authorities; and 
(e) if so, the steps taken by the RBI in such cases to safeguard the 
96 

[3 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
deposits of the public? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI ANANDRAO VITHOBA ADSUL): (a) to (c) 
Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is empowered under the Banking Regulation 
Act, 1949 to regulate functioning of all the banks in India, including foreign 
banks. All guidelines issued by RBI for regulating the functioning of banks in 
India are equally applicable to foreign banks. RBI's control over the foreign 
banks is the same as over domestic banks. 
(d) and (e) No, Sir.The foreign banks are required to give prior notice, to 
RBI, of their intention to close down their operations in India.The bank 
intending to close down its operation in India is required to discharge all its 
liabilities, realise assets and clear all obligations under contingent liabilities, 
before it is permitted by RBI to close operations in India. RBI ensures that 
foreign bank closes its operation in India only after meeting all liabilities in 
India including liabilities to depositors and investors.

Report on safe drinking water 
1504. SHRI CR THIRUNAVUKKARASU: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have taken note of the report published by Third 
World Academy of Science on 'Safe Drinking Water'; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c)whether it is a fact that India has to face severe water scarcity as per the 
report; and 
(d) if so, the action proposed by Government to deal with the situation? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The report published by Third World Academy of Science on "Safe 
Drinking Water" states that the majority of the world's population does not 
have access to safe drinking water. This is certainly true in most parts of 
Africa and Asia. Even in relatively adva nced countries such as India, safe 
drinking water is not readily available, particularly in rural areas. Together 
these sources account for just 1 per cen t of all water on earth. Six billion 
people depend on freshwater supply (available from rivers, lakes, 
underground sources and aquifers) and a significant portion of the world's 
population now face water shortages. Today 31 countries representing 2.8 
billion people, including China, India, Kenya, Ethiopia, Nigeria and Peru, 
confront chronic water problems. Total withdrawals of freshwater have 
increased dramatically in 
165 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
RAJYA SABHA [3 December, 2002] 
recent times. The groundwater aquifers are currently being depleted faster 
than they are being replenished in parts of India, China and the United States. 
The report narrates some success stories of augmenting supply of water and 
water harvesting and community farming in Rajasthan achieved by Tarun 
Bharat Sangh. The report also speaks about ways to save and replenish water, 
making water safe and potable, making waste water fit for use again and 
technology to make safe drinking water. 
(c) The average annual water availability in the river-systems of the 
country is assessed at 1869 Billion C ubic Metre (BCM). According to the 
International Criteria, a situation of annual water availability of less than 1000 
cubic metre per capita is considered as scarcity condition. The per capita 
water availability in India is 1820 cubic metre per year (2001). However, due 
to spatial variability of rain in the co untry and also because of variation in 
population density, per capita average annual availability of water in different 
basins presently varies from 16,990 cubic metre in Minor River Basins draining 
into Bangladesh & Myanmar, 13,636 cubic metre in Brahmaputra-Barak basin 
to 298 cubic metre in Sabarmati basin. Presently, per capita water availability 
in some river basins namely. Area of  Inland Drainage in Rajasthan Desert; 
Sabarmati; East Flowing Rivers between Mahanadi and Kanyakumari; Pennar; 
West Flowing Rivers of Kutchh, Saurashtra including Luni; Cauvery; Tapi and 
Mahi is in scarcity cdondition. Further, temporal variability in rainfall also 
creates temporary scarcity of water in certain years. In year 2025, the per 
capita water availability has been estimated as 1341 cubic metre per year on a 
national level. The river basins Krishna, Subarnarekha and Ganga are also 
likely to come under the category ot scarce basins. 
(d) To address the problem of water scarcity in the country, emphasis is 
being made to augmei*:t storages through constructioa of dams, speedy 
completion of ongoing water resources projects, other means for water 
harvesting and conservation, and non-conventionaJ measures like interlinking 
of rivers. The National Perspective Plan for water resources development 
envisages interlinking between various Peninsular rivers and Himalayan rivers 
for transfer of water from surplus basins to water deficit basins to provide 
benefits of drinking water supply, irrigation, hydro-power, flood control, 
navigation, fisheries, salinity and pollution control etc. 
166 

[3 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
Water Supply is a State subject and State Governments implement 
schemes/projects on drinking water supply from their own resources. The 
Government of India supplements their efforts to overcome the water crisis by 
providing financial assi stance under the Accelerated Rural Water Supply 
Programme (ARWSP).

Distress sale of Paddy by farmers In Andhra Pradesh 
DR. DASARI NARAYANA RAO (Andhra Pradesh): Madam Deputy 
Chairman, this year, my home State, Andhra Pradesh, has experienced the 
w/orst drought. As reported, the rainfall was 34 per cent less than the normal 
rainfall. Despite this, the paddy grower s have grown their crop in whatever 
way they can. Normally, 7 million tonnes of paddy is grown in the State, but 
it is estimated that this year, the paddy yield is around 48 lakh tonnes only, 
which has affected the farmers very ba dly. But the miseries of the hapless 
farmers are far from over, as the paddy is lying unsold with them. There are 
no takers for the paddy in the State. The Food Corporation of India is not 
purchasing the paddy under one pretext or the other. The rice mill owners too 
are reluctant to purchase the paddy, l eaving the farmers high and dry. Thus, 
practically, the MSP declared for paddy has become redundan t in the State. 
The paddy farmers have started distress sale of their produce, resulting in a 
great loss to the farmers of the State. 
1, therefore, earnestly appeal to the Central Government to come to 
the rescue of the poor paddy growers of Andhra Pradesh and direct the FCI 
and other Government agencies to purchase the entire paddy stock of the 
farmers at the MSP declared by the Go vernment, without further loss of time, 
and save the paddy farmers of Andhra Pradesh who might resort to

Demand for upgrading Sambalpur University to Central University 
MS. PRAMII-A BOHIDAR (Orissa):  Madam Deputy Chairperson, 
the Sambalpur University serves as the chief educational centre for the entire 
western parts of Orissa. The Sambalpur University was established on is'"

India has launched the KBK Programme  in these districts to eradicate 
backwardness. The Scheduled Castes an d the Scheduled Tribes constitute 46 
per cent of the total population of this region, against the Orissa State average 
of 38 per cent and the nati onal average of 22 per cent. The Scheduled Castes,

demand for upgrading Sambalpur University to a Central University. Thank 
you.

SHRI R.S.GAVAI (Maharashtra) : Ma dam, the Gowari caste is one 
of the important Tribes and its population throughout Maharashtra is 20 lakhs. 
Major portion of this Tribe lives in nine districts of Vidarbha. Similarly, about 
ten lakh people belonging to the Gowari caste live in Madhya Pradesh. 
Various Foreign and Indian sociologists, anthropologists, research scholars 
and authorities have, after a study, accepted that the Gowari caste is one of 
the component elements of the tribal population and have given the findings 
that Gowari caste is a Tribe. Originally, in the British regime, the Gowari caste 
was listed in the Vidarbha region of Maharashtra State and the districts of 
Madhya Pradesh as Aboriginal Tribes an d they were also availing of all the 
tribal facilites. 
But due to ignorance most of the people of the Tribe could not avail 
of any facilities. The Maharashtra Government has made strong 
recommendation to the Central Government after research and detailed study 
of the backwardness of the people belonging to the Gowari caste stating that 
the Gowari caste is Tribe and it should be included in the Scheduled Tribes 
list. 
I, therefore, request the Government of India to take steps to include 
the Gowari caste in the revised Scheduled Tribes list of Maharashtra and 
extend tribal facilities to them.
