SHRI J. CHITHARANJAN (Kerala): Mr. Vice-Chairman. Sir, I 
support the Statutory Resolution that this House disapproves the Unit Trust of 
India fTransferof Undertaking and Repeal) Ordinance, 2002. 
Sir, I also opposed the Unit Trust of India fTransfer of Undertaking 
and Repeal) Bill, 2002, 
Sir, the Unit Trust of India was established with certain noble 
objectives of mobilising the savings in our country and utilise it for the 
accelerated development of our economy, In its first two or three decades, the 
UTI was functioning well and the people had extreme confidence in it 
because it was a Government undertak ing. During this period it had a 
tremendous growth and it emerged as the tallest mutual fund organisation in 
the whole country. But for the last few years, it has been in crisis, it has 
landed into trouble. I need not go into the details. But these are all man made 
situations. All these points are being looked into by the Joint Parliamentary 
Committee. What I understand is that the Committee has almost finalised its 
report and it is to be submitted within the next few days. Naturally, the 
Committee may mention the factors which led to this crisis. It may also 
suggest the steps to be taken to remedy the situation. Therefore, the 
Government could have waited till the Joint Parliamentary Committee had 
submitted its report. I do not know why the Government was so impatient in 
taking certain steps to restructure this organisation. It is always better to 
deeply look Into the problems and come to certain solutions. Instead of that, 
why should there be a haste? My request to the Government is that even now 
they can wait till the time the

Moreover, it should be considered in that background when the Government is 
thinking that we should attain economic development at the rate of a per cent

rate Is attained, we cannot solve the problems of poverty and unemployment'.

on is our own national savings. In that case, our position is very bad. We are

raise it to 30 per cent, or, even up to 40 per cent. In that case, this institution

we do not have any Extradition Treaty w ith Portugal. Therefore, immediately 
after it was informed on 19th September that Abu Salem has been arrested in 
Lisbon, — he was on our wanted list — the Minister of External Affairs wrote a 
formal letter to the Portugal Government requesting that he be extradited to India, 
because a number of cases relating to serious offences are pending against him 
in Indian courts. Subsequently, the CBI team went there.The Embassy in Lisbon 
provided full assistance to our team.The CBI team had had elaborate discussions 
with Portuguese authorities.The Portuguese authorities were, all along, helpful. At 
no point of time, did we come across any difficulty, but they said that we have 
to proceed as per law. And, as per law, a formal extradition request has to come 
from the Government of India on the cases pending against him, with the 
requisite FIRs, evidences, etc.These are required to be furnished. Furthermore, 
under the Portuguese law, there is not provision of capital punishment. And, 
they do not extradite a person who can be given capital punishment in another 
country. So, they would like to have an assurance from the Government of India 
that even after being extradited, he would not be subjected to capital 
punishment. It will require the State Governments to give all the necessary 
evidence and get it translated in Portuguese. All this process takes its own 
time. They have assured us that, at the moment, he is being tried or he is being 
investigated in relation to offences committed there in Portugal under the 
violation of the law of immigration and so many other laws. They have said 
that 'you may rest assured that we are not going to release him, and, in the 
meanwhile, you complete your process.' They have taken a remand of 90 days. So, 
within those 90 days, the process required from the Government of India would 
be completed. And, we are hopeful that Abu Salem would be extradited to India.

be pleased to state: 
(a) whether insurance schemes have been extended to the handloom weavers 
of Andhra Pradesh; 
(b) if so, the number of weavers covered under the schemes as on date,

(d) the role being played by Central and State Governments in this 
regard?

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF TEXTILES 
(SHRI BASANGOUDA R. PATIL): (a) to  (d) A statement is laid on the 
Table of House. 
Statement 
(a) Till the end of the IX Plan, the Government of India had been 
implementing a Group Insurance Scheme and a New Insurance Scheme for 
Handloom Weavers in the country including the State of Andhra Pradesh. The State 
Government of Andhra Pradesh had a availed itself of Central assistance under 
the Group Insurance Scheme. Howeve r, the State Government had not 
implemented the New Insurance Scheme during the years 2000-01 and 2001-02. 
(b)The information on district-wise number of weavers covered under the 
Group Insurance Scheme during the year 2001-02 is given in the Statement 
(See below). 
(c) and (d) Under the Group Insurance Scheme, the insurance cover per 
weaver was of Rs. 10,000/- for an annu al premium was shared equally by the 
beneficiary, the State Government and the Central Government. The scheme 
covered natural death of the weaver and was implemented in collaboration with 
the Life Insurance Corporation of India. The New Insurance Scheme 
implemented through United India Insurance Co. Ltd. (UIIC) provided a 
coverage of Rs. 1.00 lakh in the event of death or loss of two limbs or two eyes 
or permanent disability due to accident. It also provided for a coverage of Rs. 
50,000/- for loss of one limb or one eye. Under the scheme, insurance coverage 
was available in respect of damage of dwelling unit and raw materials also. The 
premium was Rs. 120/- per annum, with a contribution of Rs. 20/- by the weaver, 
Rs. 40/- by the State Government and Rs. 60/- by the Government of India. 
In accordance with the announcemen t made by the Hon'ble Prime 
Minister in his Independence Day address to the Nation on the 15th August, 2002, a 
special contributory insurance scheme for weavers and artisans combining the 
Janshree Bima Yojana administered by the Life Insurance Corporation with the 
Group Insurance Scheme has been included as a component in a 
comprehensive Weavers' Welfare Scheme, for

implementation during the Tenth Plan and the draft scheme has since been sent to the 
Planning Commission as per the prescribed procedure for appraisal.

*232. SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: Will the Minister of HOME 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have any proposal to constitute a Central 
Negotiating Division to tackle hostage situations instead of commando

(c) if not, the reasons therefor; and 
(d) the details of any groundwork done by the Central Government in this 
direction? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI CHENNAMANENI VIDYA SAGAR RAO): (a) There is no such 
proposal under consideration. 
(b) Does not arise. 
(c) and (d) There exists a contingency plan to deal with any hostage 
situation in Civil Aviation. In regard to other hostage situations, the primary 
responsibility rests with the State Governments. The Central Government has 
however, recently intiated action to orga nize Hostage Negotiations Courses at 
National Police Academy (SVPNPA) at Hyderabad for security for police 
personnel including those from the States.

hon. Minister is this. The hostage problem is becoming a universal problem, 
and, particularly, in our country, terrorism has become a very common thing. If 
you do not have any definite plan of action, do you have any alternative 
programme to tackle this menace effectively, without affecting the life of the 
people who have been taken as hostages? 
DEPUTY PRIME MINISTER, IN-CHARGE OF THE MINISTRY OF 
HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI L.K. ADVANI): Madam, the hon. Member is right. 
There is an increasing inci dence of terrorism and terrorists have very often 
made certain vulnerable sections host ages. Recently, we had a very ugly 
incident in Moscow. Therefore, the pr emier institution in the country which 
gives training to police personnel, the National Police Academy, has recently 
visited that place also. They have undertaken a

Terrorist activities from Bhutan 
*222.  SHRI SURESH KALMADI: 
SHRI KARNENDU BHATTACHARJEE: 
Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of the fact that the militants are 
carrying on terrorist activities on a large scale from Bhutan alongwith the 
Assam-Bhutan border; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the steps taken/proposed to be taken in 
this regard? 
(c) whether the Central Government have received any request from the 
State Government of Assam to flush out National Democratic Font for Bodoland 
(N.D.F.B.) militants; if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) Government's reaction thereto and steps contemplated in this 
direction? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY FOR HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI I.D. SWAMI) :(a) to (d) The Government is aware about the existence of 
camps of Indian insurgent groups including National Democratic Front of 
Bodoland (NDFB) in Bhutan territory, which are being used by them for safe 
havens, sanctuary, training purposes and launching of operations against 
Indian civilians and security forces. The Government of Assam have also 
drawn the attention of the Central Government in this regard. 
The matter regarding removal of camps of Indian insurgent groups from 
Bhutan territory has been taken up from time to time with the Royal 
Government of Bhutan (RGOB). The issue was also discussed in detail during 
the visits of External Affairs Minister of Bhutan from August 4 to 6, 2002 and 
Foreign Secretary from October 28 to 30, 2002, with the Bhutanese 
leadership. The RGOB have assured that they will not allow these elements to 
use their territory for activities prejudicial to the interests of India.

Rehabilitation package for riot victims in Gujarat 
*225. SHRI RAJKUMAR DHOOT: Will the Minister of HOME 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government prepared a rehabilitation 
package for riot affected people of Gujarat; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the reasons for delay in finalising the package? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI I.D. SWAMI): (a) to (c) Besides the efforts undertaken by Government 
of Gujarat for rehabilitation of riot affected people, the Prime Minister announced 
on April 30,2002 a Package of Rs. 150 crores for the ec onomic rehabilitation 
for the riot-affected persons in Gujarat which included: 
(i)   Reconstruction and repair of damaged homes and shops both in rural 
and urban areas. 
(ii)   Assistance to all the self-employed categories who lost their 
earning assets. 
(iii) Financial support for recommending business, commercial and 
industrial activities. 
(iv) Revival of educational, medical and other institutions in the 
affected areas and special progr ammes to benefit widows and 
children. 
The package announced by the Prime Minister supplemented the 
schemes udertaken by the Govt, of Gujarat and is being implemented 
expeditiously. There has been no delay in finalising the package. 
Assistance to SERCs 
*228. SHRI S.M. LAL JAN BASHA: Will the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have a plan to assist the State Electricity 
Regulatory Commission, based on their performance; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
31 

RAJYA SABHA [4 December, 2002] 
(c) whether money has been released to any State Electricity 
Regulatory Commission under this incentive scheme; and 
(d) if so, the details of funds released? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI ANANT GANGARAM GEETE): (a) 
to (d) As per the provisions of the Electricity Regulatory Commissions (ERC) 
Act, 1998, the responsibility of constitution and funding of State Electricity 
Regulatory Commissions (SERCs) vests with the State Government. The 
SERCs are constituted by the State Governments in terms of Section 17 of the 
ERC Act. As regards the budget of the State Commission, the ERC Act 
provides that the State Commissions shall prepare, in such form and at such 
time in each financial year as may be prescribed, its budget for the next 
financial year, showing the estimated re ceipts and expenditure of the State 
commission and forward the same to the State Government. 
Union Government has no plan for extending financial assistance to State 
Electricity Regulatory Commissions (SERCs) nor of evaluating their 
performance. 
Financial assistance to some SERCs has been provided by the Power 
Finance Corporation (PFC) in the form of grant to promote Reforms in the States.

Statement 
Details of the Power Sector Reform Fund 
As a part of measures to refo rm the power sector, the Committee 
recommended that State Government should consolidate the past liabilities and 
finance them through agreements for write-downs and future sector surpluses. 
However, going by the track record of State Governments, a mere statement of 
intent is unlikely to carry any weight from the other stakeholders, specifically 
existing creditors and prospective lenders. In order to enhance the credibility and 
mitigate the risk of policy reversals it is necessary to ring-fence both the 
liabilities and the inflows earmarked for the sector restructuring. In order to do 
this, the State Government should establish a Power Sector Reform Fund 
(PSRF). All existing liabilities of the sector should be transferred to the PSRF. 
The responsibility for servicing these liabilities, however, remains with the 
State Government and as noted later, these can be re-financed on better terms 
with Central Government support. Conc omitantly, existing receivables (the 
privatized utility can be contracted to recover them the on an incentive-sharing 
basis), privatisation proceeds, and gran ts from the Government of India and 
other donor agencies should be transferred to the PSRF to defray these 
liabilities. In addition, it wo uld receive a portion of the surplus from future 
operations as revenues, say, in the form of a PSRF surcharge, The PSRF 
would be drawn Upon in a pre-specified order of priority to meet the State 
Government's obligations in discharging its liabilities.

by the EU 
1618. SHRI PARMESHWAR KUMAR AGARWALLA: Will the Minister 
of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that European Union has rejected the draft of the 
Delhi Declaration circulated by the Indian Government at the climate change 
meet; 
(b) if so, what are the details of the draft circulated; and 
(c) what are the reasons given by the European Union for rejecting it? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) to (c) The European Union did not 
reject the draft of the Delhi Declaration. A group of developed countries, 
including the European Union wanted to initiate a process for beginning a 
dialogue on broader participation of countries in greenhouse gas mitigation 
commitments for period beyond 2012. This  was resisted successfully by the 
developing countries, including India, on the grounds that the per capita 
greenhouse gas emissions of the developing countries, in general, were low in 
comparison to the developed countries, and that the overriding priority for the 
developing countries was poverty eradication for which economic growth was 
essential. The Delhi Ministerial Declaration on Climate Change and Sustainable 
Development was adopted by all Parties as a consensus document.

†1628. SHRI DILIP SINGH JUDEV: Will the Minister of RURAL

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI ANNASAHEB M.K. PATIL): (a) to (e) Drinking 
water supply being a State subject, schemes for providing drinking water 
facilities are implemented by the State Governments from their own 
resources.The Government of India supp lements the efforts of the States by 
providing financial assistance under the Accelerated Ru ral Water Supply 
Programme (ARWSP).The powers to plan, sanction and implement Rural Water 
Supply schemes under the above programes rests with the State Governments. 
Details of individual water supply scheme in the States are not maintained by the 
Central Government. However, as per information furnished by the Government 
of Chhattisgarh, there are 25,301 handpumps in the State under rural water supply 
programme. 
Annexure showing release and expenditure under Accelerated Rural Water 
Supply Programme including activities taken under DPP for the  
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
156 

[4 December, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
last five years, State-wise, is enclosed [See Appendix 197 Annexure No. 14]. 
Annexure showing expenditure under State Sector programme for Rural Water 
Supply during the last five years is enclosed. [See Appendix 197 Annexure No. 
15] 
The following noms and criteria are being adopted under Accelerated Rural 
Water Supply Programme for providing drinking water to rural population in 
the habitations: 
(a) 40 liters per capita per day (Ipcd) of safe drinking water for human 
beings. 
(b) 30 Ipcd additional for cattle in the Desert Development Programme 
Areas. 
(c) One hand-pump or stand post for every 250 persons. 
(d) The water source should exist within the habitation/within 1.6 km in the 
plains and within 100 mtrs. elevation in the hilly areas. 
[Water is defined as safe if it is free from biological contamination 
(guinea worms, cholera, typhoid etc.) and chemical contamination (excess fluoride, 
brackishness, iron, arsenic, nitrates)] 
Recently Government of India have approved the relaxations in the rural 
water supply norms in the following manner: - 
(a) The norms may be relaxed to provide for 55 Itrs. per capita per day 
with a source within 0.5 km in the plains and 50 metres elevation in 
the hills after the coverage of a ll Not Covered and Partially Covered 
rural habitations in that State is achieved, as per the existing norms of 
40 litres per capita per day. This relaxation is subject to the condition that 
beneficiaries of the relaxed norms will share a part of the capital cost 
(which should not be less than 10%) and shoulder full responsibilities 
for subsequent Operation and Maintenance. 
(b) In case of schemes in quality affe cted villages or in multi-village 
schemes where the capital cost is very high, the schemes could be 
executed and implemented by the Government Departments/ 
Agencies/Board, and water is supplied to individual villages at 
157 

RAJYA SABHA [4 December, 2002] 
the periphery of each village. For drinking water distribution within the 
village, the beneficiaries would share a part of the capital cost (which 
should not be less than 10%) and shoulder full responsibilities for 
subsequent Operation and Maintenance of the village water distrbution 
network, while Government Department/ Board/Agency would maintian 
the main water supply system upto the village. 
Governments/Board/Agency may also charge water rates to the 
Panchayats/Village communities for bulk supply of water for drinking 
purpose. Such water charges and the village Operation and 
Maintenance cost would be fully met by the users/ beneficiaries. 
As per recent information available out of 50,379 rural habitations in 
Chhattisgarh all habitations have been fully covered and there are no Not 
Covered and Partially Covere d habitations in the State. This information is, 
however, provisional and subject to revision.

the Technology Upgradation Fund Scheme (TUFS). For providing incentives for 
exporters, the External Market Assistance (EMA) Scheme has been extended for

SHORT DURATION DISCUSSION 
On Disinvestment of Public Sector Undertakings 
SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE (W est Bengal): Madam Deputy 
Chairperson, I express my gratitude to you for allowing me to raise the 
discussion on disinvestment of public sector undertakings under Rule 176. 
Madam, we have discussed the issue of disinvestment a number of 
times and mostly through the initiative taken by the private. Members. So far 
as the Government's position is concerne d, almost in every year's B'udget, 
they indicate a figure in the Budget documents that certain amounts will be 
realised through the disinv estment process. And, most of the times, we find, 
at the end of the year, when the Re vised estimates are made available, 
through the Budget documents, those targets remain unfulfilled and we are 
nowhere near the targeted figures, which were projected at the initial stage of 
the Budget. We are not going to discu ss the Tenth Five-Year Plan, as it has 
not yet been approved by the N.D.C. But, what we find that Rs.78,000 crores 
will be realised through the route of disinvestment. The contemporary events, 
and also the sharp differences in the Council of Ministers on the issue of 
disinvestment,' as reported in the news papers, we find that apart from the 
concept of joint responsibility, sacrificing in a parliamentary form of 
Government. It raises substantial issues is not desirable that Ministers should 
express their views, air their individual opinions, publicly.   But, those were 
the traditions of the past.   We are living 
193 

RAJYA SABHA [4 December, 2002] 
in a new regime, where each and every individual Minister expresses his 
views, irrespective of the position taken by the Cabinet, as a whole. However, 
this time this practice raises substantial policy matters which we should 
discuss I would ndt like to go through the entire process. I will be a little 
selective. We find in the Press on the 2 nd September, 2002, and I quote that 
the Defence Minister, while opposing th e process of disinvestment observed, 
"Public sector undertakings have come into existence on tax-payers' money. 
The assets thus created should not be handed over to corporate sector, to 
create private monopoly. Let us assume a PSU becomes a monopoly, but on 
the plea that PSU is a monopoly, you cannot create a private sector 
monopoly." It is followed by Shri Ram Naik, as the newspaper report on 8th of 
September, "He is strongly against the disinvestment of HPCL and BPCL to 
private firms before a proper system to stabilise the r ecently de-regulated 
sector to disrupt the supplies, as it could stall the present barter system 
between the oil firms." These are all the reports published in newspapers, in 
the month of September alone. On 17 th of September, another Union Minister 
joins the headline of The Asian Age of that day, "Union Minister Dhindsa 
opposes privatisation of profit-making fertilizer company." He is followed by 
another Minister, Minister in-charge of  Heavy Industries, Shri V.K.Patil. He 
writes a letter to the Prime Minister, and before the letter reaches the desk of 
the Prime Minister, we find a news item in The Statesman on 18 th of 
September, that he opposes the disinvestment, as strategic sale of the PSU was 
opposed by his party supremo. Then, HRD Minister does not lag behind. He 
also joins the issue and he ultimately convenes a meeting with some of his - if 
I use the word, if I am permitted to us e the word - "fellow travellers", and 
they evolve a strategy of how to oppose the disinvestment process. 
On 3rd October, the RSS Chief thunders and the report this appeared 
in the Indian Express of that day -- " Sack all those who are against 
Swadeshi". And, ultimately, we found the Prime Minister's intervention in a 
very feeble, oblique manner when his Council of Ministers were expressing 
their divergent views on disinvestment, a major policy of the Government of 
India. We find that on 6 th October and there is a newspaper item on 6 th 
October, while addressing the full Planning Commission and endorsing the 
figure, which I have already quoted, that during the Tenth Plan period, 
Rs.78,000 crores are to be mobilised, through disinvestment he hardened his 
position on reforms.  This is the point which I 
194 

[4 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
would like to emphasise. I would like to know from the Government: Do they 
consider that disinvestment is the core of economic reforms, that privatisation 
is the core of economic reforms, distancing itself from industrial and 
economic activity and keeping the Governme nt of the day neutral is the core 
of economic reforms? These are some of the basic issues which are to be 
answered. And, precisely because of that, we thought that a discussion should 
be raised on the floor of this House. 
Before I come to certain other asp ects, I would like to point out one 
thing very clearly. Very often, rather, more than often, it is pointed out, "The 
policies which we are pursuing, are the extension of the policies which 
Congress initiated." I thank them, thos e who say it, because while sitting on 
this side, they opposed those measures tooth and nail, including the decision 
of signing the World Trade Agreement on 14 th April, 1994. But it is not 
correct; the policies which are being pursued, are not the extension of the 
policies which were initiated by the Congress during the years 1991-96. To 
remove this misunderstanding, we must clearly point out and spell out what is 
the difference between the policies wh ich they are pursuing and what our 
perception was, what we did and what we  wanted to do. Madam, in regard to 
disinvestment, Dr. Manmohan Singh made the first policy statement, while 
presenting his Budget on 24 th July, 1991. I quote from his Budget speech. He 
observed: "In order to raise resources, encourage wider public participation 
and promote greater accountability, up to 20 per cent of the Government 
equity in selected public sector undertakings would be offered to mutual 
funds, investment institutions in the public sector and also to the workers in 
these firms. That was the policy of disinvestment which was initiated by Dr. 
Manmohan Singh. Is that the policy being pursued today? No. These were the 
conditions under which we articulated our policies. Even in January, 2001, we 
adopted a document, titled "Summary of the recommendations of Economic 
Introspection Group" which is the basic document in regard to disinvestment; 
-- I am not going to read out the details - it is a public document published by 
AICC anybody can have it -- where In pages 21-23, we have discussed in 
detail our approach to disinvestment. We have made it quite clear that no 
profit-making public sector undertakings should be disinvested. If they enjoy 
monopoly, create level play ground for all in a competitive atmosphere. If 
they earn profit in a comparable situation, there is no reason, why they should 
be disinvested and for what purpose. 
195 

RAJYA SABHA [4 December, 2002] 
Secondly, there must be made a distinction between those public 
sector enterprises, which were set up by the Union Government and which 
were ultimately taken over under IDR Act and those which were originally in 
the private sector and because of the si ckness in the private sector, the Union 
Government had to undertake, like a large number of textile mills, engineering 
works, transport organisations, plantations etc. They were not originally 
established by the Union Government, they were in the private sector and 
when they become sick under the priv ate sector, to protect the employees 
interest, they were taken over. In our system, we could not provide the social 
security and I am talking of the early 70s, when there were not even this much 
of social security as available today. In order to protect the job opportunities 
of the workers and to make an effort to make them viable, those were taken

SHRI LALIT SURI: The last 12 years have witnessed the impact of 
liberalisation on the Indian economy. The process of liberalisation has 
redefined the role of the State and its relationship with business. Under an 
economy which was managed predominantly by the State, there were several   
businesses  that   the   State   itself did.      However,   this  trend  has 
243 

RAJYA SABHA [4 December, 2002] 
changed the world over. The Government has never been the best of a 
business person. Bureaucrats are trained to be defensive, whereas businessmen 
are trained to be aggressive and competitive in the market. In areas in which 
the Government has had to compete with the private sector, where monopolies 
of the State have been dismantled, over  the price mechanism is not regulated 
by the State, the Government has not been able to survive competition with the 
private sector.. 
I have had some personal experience in the field of tourism and hotel 
industry. The failure of the Government in this area, in running hotels, is in 
sharp contrast to the privat e sector, which, in India, has been able to operate 
hotels considered to be amongst the best in the world. 
The basis philosophy behind disinvestment or privatisation is --where 
should the tax-payers' money be spent? Should the tax payers' money be 
invested in businesses in running hotels, in manufacturing steel, aluminium' 
and textiles, or, should it be used for the social sector to expand the base of 
education, health care, irrigation and other needs of the common man? The 
experience in these businesses has been that the Government taxes the people, 
invests his money in businesses, then loses this money. It then again taxes the 
people, draws out restructuring packages, most of which have not proved to be 
successful. In fact, it is the greatest in justice to a common man that his money 
is lost in business. In this context I quote an example of the U.K. experience 
where after disinvestment, merely the corporate tax realisation at the rate of 35 
per cent on profits brought in more money, than the total 100 per cent profits 
realised before disinvestment of these St ate enterprises. In addition, the U.K. 
Treasury made tens of billions of pounds from the sale of these companies and 
this money helped them to reduce taxes over many years, to make U.K. one of 
the lowest taxed countries in Europe. This also boosted consumer spending 
leading to higher growth and employment across the board in the economy. 
Even in our own country in the case of Modern Bread, Balco, CMC 
and others, there have been no job losses. On the other hand, higher 
production is leading to more employment directly and indirectly, higher taxes 
and other benefits to the economy. In fact, it is a win-win situation all the way.

Today, on account of borrowings of the State, necessitated by huge 
budget deficits and capital requirements for development, large amount of 
interest has to be paid by the Government. The national debt is huge. Should 
not national resources be invested in businesses, be unlocked and used to 
retire the public debt? Should this money be lost in running hotels or 
manufacturing textiles, or should this money be used to build roads, provide 
irrigation, health care and education? The choice is clear. It is not the business 
of the Government to be in business. The Government should be in the 
business in those limited sectors where the presence of the Government is 
required, on account of some strong natio nal compulsions. Either it should be 
a strategic sector, or it may be a sector where the private sector is unwilling to 
step in. 
The proceeds of the disinvestment can also be utilised to build 
physical infrastructure like roads, ports,  telecom, power etc., as well as in 
social sectors like health and educa tion. China concentrated heavily on 
investments in these sectors, which have paid very large returns by way of 
several times higher foreign investment flows as well as higher technical skills 
and productivity resulting from investments in education and health. As 
emphasised by our Nobel Laureate in Economics, Shri Amartya Sen, higher 
investments in health and education also lead to a fall in population growth 
rate and there is a total impact of all these factors on poverty reduction. 
When I look at the history of last few years, I find that there does not 
appear to be a basic conflict with the idea of disinvestment or privatisation. 
When the Congress was in power from 1991 to 1996, minority shares of 
public undertakings were sold by of f-loading into domestic and foreign 
markets. When the United Front Government was in power, the same policy 
did continue. When the NDA Government took over, it switched over to a 
mechanism of privatising public sector units through strategic sales. It is for 
the above mentioned reasons that instead of review of the disinvestment 
process, as demanded by some, we should review how disinvestment can be 
expedited. A strong political will and a basic consensus is, no doubt, required. 
Germany, after the merger, privatised 11,000 enterprises in 2 years. Not only 
should it be expedited at the Central level but also extended to the States,

DR. VIJAYA MALLYA (Karnataka): Hon. Madam Deputy 
Chairman, I thank you for this opportunity to speak. All my hon. colleagues 
have spoken with varying degrees of passion on the policy of disinvestment 
and, of course, the conduct of certain transaction relating to assets that have 
been divested. I am going to focus on disinvestment itself as a policy and 
share with this august House my view s. I am acutely aware of the time 
constraint and I shall be as brief as. I can. In my maiden speech, Madam, I 
raised the question of accountability in governan ce. Anything that the 
Government does should be as accountabl e to the elected representatives of 
the people, to the nominees of the Stat e and to the electorate themselves. I 
know that the Directive Principle of  our Constitution say that we are a 
democratic, socialist republic. . But does that mean that we are supposed to 
own manufacturing assets? The Govern ment should concentrate on areas 
where the private sector will not be interested. The 
268 

[4 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
private sector, typically the world over,  is interested in commerce. In a 
country like burs, where we have such a problem of lack of education, lack of 
adequate health facilities, poverty, I think, such sectors at affordable rates 
should be taken up by the Government and the business of running industries 
or manufacturing products should clearly be reserved for the private sector. In 
any case all the assets that we talk about, whether it is the Centaur Hotel or 
whether it is the IPCL, belong to all the taxpayers of this country. These 
assets must be put to work with a clear focus on return on investment. Merely 
saying that a particular public sector  undertaking is profitable is not a 
convincing argument because profita bility does not necessarily mean 
maximum efficiency. If we say that we  are efficient, then we must be 
competitive. We happen to have some sort of a phobia here in dealing with 
Government's intentions towards such public sector undertakings. The way to 
look at it would be to calculate the net return on investment to the 
Government. If the financial returns to the Government by privatisation, at 
whatever price, reflecting the preva iling circumstances produces a better 
return on investment as compared to the dividends that these companies pay, 
then they must be privatised. There has to be a focused economic approach 
rather than a political approach to the entire process of divestment. I would 
say that the Government should also re examine the price earning ratios of the 
public sector undertakings. My information that blue-chip public sector 
undertakings which were profitable, had a PE ratio between four and six 
times. Now these have actually risen after the divestment policy between 11 
and 85 times. This has increased the value of Government investment in the 
public sector units. If these have to be cashed out to provide a better return to 
the Government, then that is the correct policy to follow. We also have a 
phobia on monopolies and I do not understand why. There are some 
companies that have huge market shares. But equally like in the United States, 
you have the Anti-Trust laws. So, we can always protect the consumers' 
interests through regulation where exploitation is not possible. But just 
because a company is gigantic in size,  should not mean necessarily that we 
look differently at that company. It should, on the contrary, be appreciated 
that a company has achieved a world class size and economics of scale. 
Similarly, we have a phobia regarding the entry of multinationals. We seem to 
think that the sovereignty of India is threatened if large multinationals come 
and invest in our country. What is wrong if we today have several 
opportunities for IT professionals in the United States and why should we be 
worried about large companies coming into India either in the infrastructure 
269 

RAJYA SABHA [4 December, 2002] 
or petroleum or oil sector or for that matter in any business? We should 
welcome them and encourage competit ion because competition means that 
the consumers will benefit. And, there is no reason why the consumer should 
not benefit. There are too many rent seekers or, people, with vested interests, 
not only in the private sector but, we also know in the public sector as well, 
and these are the people who have their own vested interests to protect against 
privatisation or who make it a point to misrepresent the facts so that the 
privatisation policy can be criticised. It is fine to have a political debate and to 
protect political positions. But the reality of the situation is, that privatisation 
helps. In my State of Karnataka, we have invested Rs. 22,000 crores in public 
sector undertakings. One such ex ample is Mangalore Chemicals and 
Fertilizers Limited which was given to my group. Suffice it to say that we 
have implemented a Rs. 470-crore rehabilitation package and it is now a 
profit-making company. It is out of the BIFR. The Government of Karnataka 
could not run it. The MCF was on the verge of bankruptcy. And, today, we 
supply 85 per cent of the fertilizer ne eds of Karnataka State. This is one 
example of where a priv ate company can, actually, turn around what the 
public sector management had virtually run into the ground. 
Madam, the labour issue, arising ou t of privatisation, is not such a 
big issue. We have, in business, launched several Voluntary Retirement 
Schemes, which are designed to be nefit those who accept them. And, 
typically, if a private sector company takes over a public sector company -
once again, I refer to MCF -- yes; we offered a VRS. But, the remnant 
workmen, actually, were given a much better compensation package. So, to 
try to compare public sector  efficiency versus private sector efficiency is one 
thing. But to make huge capital out of it and say that divestment should not be 
pursued is something that is terribly retrograde. I may be referred to as a 
capitalist. But, nevertheless, I am an industrialist and I fully support 
privatisation and encourage the Government to use the proceeds of 
privatisation for tangible social benefits such as education and health care and 
there is really no need for the Government to be in the business of running 
industry.   Thank you.

At the beginning of the qualitative objectives are the fundamental 
principles, which I just talked about that the Government must focus on 
governance, which is where we have failed our country, largely, over the last 
fifty-five years. We have largely failed our country when it comes to primary

poverty. However, we have taken great steps in the direction of eliminating 
poverty, but we have yet eradicated it totally. This is what on which the

Statement 
The employment exchanges are under the administrative and financial control 
of the respective States/UT Governments and these are being modernized 
according to their financial capacity. At  present 363 out of 939 employment 
exchanges are computerized. 
Reliable estimates of employment and unemployment are obtained from the 
quinquennial labour force surveys conducted by the National Sample Survey 
Organisation. Job-seekers registered with the employment exchanges are not 
necessarily unemployed and it is also not necessary that all the unemployed 
should register with the employment exchanges. Therefore, the employment 
exchange data provides details of the job seekers registered and not the 
complete picture of unemployment in the country. 
SHRI PRITHVIRAJ CHAVAN: Sir, my question focuses on the statistical data 
about unemployment which is primarily obtained from the employment exchanges 
in the organised sector. Of course, in the unorganised sector, only sample surveys 
are done. So, the quality of data is hardly useful. As you know, Sir, in the 
Western countries the rate of unemploym ent is a very crucial parameter for 
the evaluation of the economy. We have no such reliable data about the exact 
number of unemployed people. The employment exchanges work at more than 
900 places and they collect data only from establishments which are employing 
more than 25 people in the organised sector. There is the Compulsory Notification 
of Vacancies Act. But the employment exchanges are monitored by the State 
Governments. What is the punitive action taken against the companies which 
do not notify vacancies? Our experience is that nobody bothers to inform the 
employment exchanges about the exis ting vacancies. They advertise the 
vacancies in the newspapers. 
MR. CHAIRMAN: You have already put your question. Let him answer. 
SHRI PRITHVIRAJ CHAVAN: I would like to know whether the 
Compulsory Notification of Vacancies Act is being followed or not.

AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of the news report captioned "Right

(b) if so, what steps would be taken to provide rice to families Living Below 
the Poverty Line as directed by the Supreme Court; 
(c) what action Government propose to take so that price of the rice through 
ration shop is fixed as per the purchasing capacity of these families living in 
extreme poverty; 
(d) whether any action plan is proposed to be formulated to help villagers 
in various parts of the country who are bracing themselves for extreme hunger 
in months ahead due to crop failure; and 
(e) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND- PUBLIC 
DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SHARAD YADAV): (a) to (e) A Statement is laid on 
the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) to (e) The Central Government have been making allocations of 
foodgrains under the Targeted Public Distribution System (TPDS) to the State 
Governments and UT Administrations for distribution amongst the BPL 
families @ 35 kg per family per month. The Central Issue Prices for the BPL 
families are highly subsidized and have remained unchanged since July, 2000. 
In order to address the needs of one crore poorest of the poor families, the 
Antyodaya Anna Yojana (AAY) is being implemented in all parts of the country 
under which foodgrains are issued @ Rs. 2 a kg for wheat and Rs. 3 a kg for 
rice at the retail level.Under the Special Component of the Sampoorna Gramin 
Rojgar Yojana (SGRY), the foodgrains are provided, free of cost, to the States 
affected by natural calamities such as flood, cyclone and drought for 
generation of additional employment oppo rtunities, alongwith food security, 
through creation of durable community assets in the rural areas. So, far, about 
38.29 lakh MTs of foodgrains have been allotted to 16 drought/natural calamity 
affected States under the Special Component of the SGRY during the current 
financial year.

†260. SHRI RAM JETHMALANI: 
SHRI RAJIV RANJAN SINGH 'LALAN':

† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
37 

RAJYA SABHA [5 December, 2002] 
(b) if so, whether Government had also finalized any policy to ascertain such 
numbers; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof and the difference between the old and new 
procedure and policy? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING 
(SHRIMATI VASUNDHARA RAJE): (a) and (b) The Planning Commission 
has been estimating the incidence of pov erty at National and State level since 
the late 1970s. The estimates of poverty were initially made from the method 
outlined in the Task Force on Projection of Minimum Needs and Effective 
Consumption Demand. Th is method was replaced by the methodology 
contained in the Report of the Expert Group on Estimation of Proportion and 
Number of Poor {commonly known as Lakdawala Committee, named after its 
Chairman) in March 1997 to estimate the poverty ratio (also known as the 
Head-Count ratio) at National and State level. According to this method, the 
percentage of people below the poverty line is estimated from state-specific 
poverty lines and state-specific consumer expenditure distribution, obtained from 
the large sample surveys on household consumer expenditure conducted by the 
NSSO once in approximately five years. Using this method, the poverty 
estimates of all the previous years have been re-worked and are available for 
the years 1973-74, 1977-78,1983,1987-88, 1993-94 and 1999-2000. 
(c) The Planning Commission in 1977 constituted a Task Force on 
Minimum Needs and Effective Consumption Demands which defined the 
poverty line as per capita expenditure level at which the average per capita per 
day calorie in take was 2400 kcal in rural areas and 2100 kcal in urban areas.The 
monetary equivalent of these norms were calculated as monthly per capita 
consumption expenditure of Rs.49.09 in rural areas and Rs. 56.64 in urban areas 
for 1973-74.These poverty lines were applied uniformly to all the States. Second, 
in order to ensure consistency with the national aggregates, the NSS consumer 
expenditure data was adjusted to the level of CSO consumption on a pro-rata basis 
across all expenditure classes. Using the poverty lines and the adjusted 
expenditure class-wise distribution of persons obtained from the national sample 
survey data on consumer expenditure of the States, the State-wise estimates of 
poverty were made. 
This methodology for estimation of poverty at National and State level 
was regarded by some as inappropriate and even inadequate in 
38 

[5 December. 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
giving a representative picture of incidence of poverty in India. In September 
1989, Planning Commission constituted an Expert Group to look into the 
methodology for estimation of poverty and to redefine the poverty line, if 
necessary. The Expert Group submitted its Report in July, 1993. 
The Expert Group did no t redefine the poverty line and accepted the one 
defined by the Task Force which was at national level. However, it 
recommended the disaggregation of the national poverty line into state-wise 
poverty lines in order to reflect the State-wise price differential. The important 
points of departure between the Expert Group methodology and the Task 
Force methodology are: 
(a) tn the new method, the NSS consumption expenditure data are not 
adjusted in any way and it is used as It is. 
(b) The new method uses State-wise poverty lines as against national level 
poverty line used in the old method. 
(c) The new method uses State-specific cost of Irving indices for updating the 
poverty line separately in rural and urban areas.The old method used only one 
all-India Index which is also same for rural and urban areas. 
The full Planning Commission under the Chairmanship of Prime Minister 
accepted its recommendations with minor modifications in March, 1997.

Disposal of nuclear waste 
1658. SHRI PARMESHWAR KUMAR AGARWALLA: Will the PRIME 
MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a) what is the present system of disposal of nuclear waste; and 
(b) whether the method followed by in the country is as per the 
international standards and the norms followed by the developed countries? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF ATOMIC 
ENERGY (SHRIMATI VASUNDHARA RAJE): (a) Radioactive wastes in 
different physical forms viz., solid, liquid and gaseous, are generated during 
operation and maintenance of nuclear reactors. The gaseous and liquid 
effluents are decontaminated by suitable treatment processes to ensure that the 
radioactive contents of the treated ef fluent are well within the permissible 
specified limits for discharge into the environment and the radioactivity is 
concentrated in small volumes. The concentrate from the liquid and solid 
wastes are immobilised in solid materials like cement, bitumen, polymers etc 
so that the radioactivity will not leach out and re-enter the bio-sphere. This 
conditioned' waste is packaged in suitable containers and placed in reinforced 
concrete trenches, tile 
47

holes and vaults, located in access controlled areas, which are under constant 
surveillance. 
(b) The method followed by India for disposal of nuclear waste is as per 
international standards and as followed by developed countries. The disposal 
operations are carried out under the surveillance of regulatory authorities.

1668. SHRI P. K. MAHESHWARI: Will the Minister of 
COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION TECHONOLGY be pleased

service in the Indian Telecom Sector has been found to be poor despite 
registering impressive growth in the past few years;

of service than BSNL and MTNL; 
(c) if so, the details of the said survey report; and 
63 

RAJYA SABHA [5 December. 2002] 
(d) the action taken by Government to improve the quality of service In the 
Indian Telecom Sector? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY (DR. 
SANJAY PASWAN): (a) Sir, the survey  conducted by TRAI through M/s. 
Indian Market Research Bureau (IMRB) during October-December 2001, has 
revealed that most of the Tetecom se rvice providers were not meeting the 
prescribed benchmarks on quality of service. 
(b) In its first quarterly survey report on quality standards, TRAI has 
found that none of the basic operators were meeting the quality of service 
(QOS) norms stipulated in the QOS regu lations of TRAI. As per the survey, 
the private operators who operate in va stly different scale of operation and 
have hardly any significant presence in the rural areas where the problems of 
maintenance are more complex, have been able to provide comparatively 
better quality of services than MTNL & BSNL. Also, while MTNL & BSNL 
have the legacy equipment, the private operators have latest technology 
equipment and gadgets. Noticeably, TRAI survey has also found that the five 
best performers in the area of basic serv ices on the basis of weighted average 
score for various customers satisfaction parameters, are the MTNL, Mumbai 
and four circles of BSNL viz. Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Gujarat and 
Andhra Pradesh. 
(c) As part of the TRAI's mandate to conduct periodical surveys for 
determining quality of Telecom services in the country, the Authority had 
selected M/s. Indian Market Resear ch Bureau (IMRB), a well established 
research organisation to perform the following two functions: 
 
> objective assessment of quality for service provided by both basic 
as well as cellular service providers  with reference to the Quality 
of service (QOS) standards prescribed by the TRAI. 
> Subjective survey of the level of consumer satisfaction with the 
services. 
The first quarterly survey was carried out during the period from October 
to December 2001. A sample size of 317 exchanges of basic service operators 
and all cellular service operators were covered in the survey. The overall 
performance of the basic service operators were 
64 

[5 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
assesed on the basis of some select parameters such as customer complaints 
on phone faults, percentage of new connections given in fifteen days, shifting 
completed within five days, closures in 24 hours, level of operator service 
response, average time taken to attend customer complaints, percantage of bills 
disputed by customers etc. In the case of cellular services, besides fault and 
billing complaints percentage of calls dropped during conversation, 
percentage of calls with good quality of voice were some of the parameters 
measured. 
The consumers surveyed generally felt that the overall quality of service 
needs to be improved. Level of satisfaction regarding service provision, 
network performance and help services were found to be very low. The 
survey findings also suggest that none of the basic operators including the 
incumbents, are meeting the QOS norms stipulated in the QOS regulations. 
(d) Actions being taken by BSNL & MTNL to improve quality of 
Telecom. Services. Improvement in the quality of service is a continuous 
process. Following steps are being taken by BSNL & fvlTNL to improve the 
basic services : 
(i)     Replacement of underground paper core cables by Jelly filled 
cables. 
(ii)      Lying of cables in ducts. 
(iii) Laying of underground cables right up to the subscribes premises so 
as to eliminate drop wires. Introduction of 5 pair undergorund 
cable is one such move in this regard. 
(iv) Opening of more and more remote line units thereby reducing area to 
be served by each exchange with a corresponding reduction in the 
size of the outdoor plant. 
(v)     Replacement of old telephone instruments. 
{vij Introduction ot new technology e.g. Wireless in Local Loop, DLC, 
etc. to eliminate the need for underground cables. 
(vii) Periodic dressing of external plant. 
(viii) Pagers to line staff/field staff wherever feasible. 
(ix) Mopttonng of faults by senior officers. 
(x) Arrangement for fault booking on 198 centrally at Short 
65

Distance Charging Centre (SDCC) on Interactive Voice Response 
Systenr) (IVRS). 
(xi) Computerisation of Fault Repair Service (FRS) at more & more 
places. 
In addition, MTNL is taking following steps to improve quality of Cellular 
Mobile Services : 
(i)     A dedicated network management group has been deployed. 
(ii) Continuous monitoring through drive tests is being carried out and 
RF optimisation is done to improve RF signal strength. 
-(ili)     The software bugs in billing system have been removed and 
regular bills are being issued. 
(iv) To improve customer interface, a full fledged call centre with IVRS 
facility is being set up. In addition to existing three Customer Care 
Centres, another five Customer Care Centres are being opened.

1673. SHRI JANARDHANA POOJ ARY : Will the Minister of 
COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY be pleased to 
state : 
(a) whether It is a fact that there is possibility to increase teledensity 
through WLL technology at comparatively lesser cost than the fixed 
telephone lines; 
69 

RAJYA SABHA [5 December, 2002] 
(b) if so, the details thereof with elucidation in comparative terms the salient 
features of the fixed line telephone and WLL-technology based telephone; 
(c) the steps taken by Government to increase the tele-density adopting 
WLL technology within the next two financial year; 
 
(d) whether Government are considering to achieve the target through 
reduced rent and tariff on WLL based telephones; and 
(e) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY (DR. 
SANJAY PASWAN) : (a) and (b) WLL (Wireless in Local Loop) is playing an 
Important role in deployment of telephones in the country. However, it is not 
possible to establish a definite correlation between tele-density and the cost of 
provision of WLL as tele-density depends upon provision of telephones which 
in turn depends upon demands for telephones. The salient features of fixed 
lines telephones and WLL technology based telephones are : 
In fixed line telephones, connections are provided through a pair of 
normally copper cable to each subs criber, whereas in WLL system 
connections are provided on wireless technology Laying of underground cable is 
time consuming, whereas WLL deployment is fast. Interruption in service will 
be there whenever cable is cut in fixed line connections due to man 
made/natural calamities, whereas interruption in WLL are not dependent on 
such eventualities except equipment fault. Fixed line telephone on copper cable 
are able to provide higher data rates compared to the presently deployed WLL 
systems though in future deployments this difference will disappear. 
(c) The Government through its Public sector units i.e. Bharat Sanchar 
Nigam Limited (BSNL) & Mahanagar Telephone Nigam Limited (MTNL) 
are planning to deploy 29^7 lakh lines on WLL during the next two 
financial years.

(TRAI) who have absolute powers to fix it and Government has no rote 
in tariff fixation.

1696. SHRI K. RAHMAN KHAN: Will the Minister of CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of the quantum of dues the sugar mills in the country owe to 
the sugarcane growers, State-wise; and 
(b) the steps taken to ensure clearance of dues by the sugar mills in a time 
bound programme to avert unhappy situation? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI V. SREENIVASA 
PRASAD): (a) A statement showing State-wise position of sugarcane price 
payable, price paid and the balance outstanding for the season 2001 -2002, as 
on 30.9.2002 is annexed. {See below) 
(b) The responsibility for ensuring timely payment of cane price dues lies 
with the State Governments which have necessary powers and field 
organizations to enforce such payments. The Central Government on its part, 
besides writing to the State Governments from time to time for expeditious 
clearance of the same, has taken the fo llowing remedial measures to improve 
the financial health of domestic sugar industry with a view to enabling it to 
reduce the cane price arrears: 
(i) The levy obligation of domestic sugar factories was reduced from 40% 
to 30% with effect from 01.01.2000 and, subsequently, to 15% with 
effect from 01.02.2001; this has further been reduced to 10% with effect 
from 01.03.2002 and will enable the sugar factories to sell more 
sugar under free sale quota In the open market and obtain better 
realization. 
(ii) To restrict the inflow of imported sugar in the country, the Central 
Government (with effect from 09.02.2000) has increased the 
customs duty to 60% along with the existing countervailing duty of 
Rs. 850 per tonne. 
103 

RAJYA SABHA [5 December, 2002] 
(iii) The Central Government is pursuing a policy of encouraging stability and 
reasonable level of sugar prices in the domestic market through judicious 
releases of free sale sugar quotas to enable the sugar factories to clear 
the cane price dues of the farmers. 
(iv) In order to liquidate the stocks of the sugar mills, the Government has 
allowed export of sugar. The quantitative ceiling on export of sugar as 
well as the requirement of registration with Agricultural and 
Processed Food Products Export Development Authority (APEDA) 
have been dispensed with, with effect from 01.04.2001. 
(v) In order to encourage the export of sugar, the Sugar Development Fund 
(SDF) Act, 1982 and the SDF Rules, 1983 have been amended, 
enabling reimbursement of the inte rnal transport & freight charges 
on export shipments of sugar. 
(vi) The Government has decided to create a buffer stock of 20 lakh tonnes 
of sugar for a period of one year. This will enable the sugar mills to 
get a subsidy amount of Rs. 412 crore from the Sugar Development 
Fund. In addition, an amount of Rs. 374 crores would be available 
from the banks to the mills on account  of buffer stock. Thus, a total 
amount of Rs. 786 crores would be provided to the mills enabling 
them to clear the payment of cane price dues to the sugarcane growers. 
This will also help the sugar industry to mitigate the financial 
hardship.

economy;

economy?

cement, steel, petroleum and oil, equipment, crushing and mixing etc. The

growth.

consumers of steel and building materials and generates employment 
opportunities.Construction of Phase I of National Highways Development 
Project (NHDP), which is presently under progress, alone requires about 30-40 
lakh tonnes of cement per year and about 3 lakh tonnes of steel per year. It would

in growth of cement industry by 9.3% and that of steel industry by 7.3% during 
period April to October 2002. 
(c) The major impact of road construction programmes would be as under 
(i) Connectivity and mobility.

ance of the Comprehensive Policy Package announced by the Hon'ble Prime

enhanced from Rs. 50 lakhs to Rs. 1 crore. The same limit is continuing since

(c) and (d) Yes, Sir. The Ministry of Finance and Company Affairs has 
informed that as per entry 54, List II in the Seventh Schedule to the

SSIs Role in Economy 
1780. SHRI SURESH PACHOURI: Will the Minister of SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of the role played by the small scale Industries in the 
economy today; 
(b) how it differs from the role played in seventies and eighties; 
(c) whether its role has diminished due to liberalisation of the  economy; 
and 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES (SHRIMATI VASUNDHARA RAJE): (a) and (b) The small 
scale industries have been playing a significant role in the Indian economy in terms 
of industrial productton, employment generation and exportsThe role of the SSI 
sector has not changed since the seventies and eighties. At present, the SSI sector 
contributes 39% of industrial production, 34% in national exports and provided 
employment to over 192 lalth persons in 2001-02. 
(c) and (d) No, Sir. In fact, the sector has emerged as a vibrant constituent ot the 
economy and is well equipped to face the challenge of liberalisation. A 
Comprehensive Policy Pacitage announced in August, 2000 contains several 
measures to further strengthen this sector both domestically and globally. The 
SSI sector has been assigned an important role in employment generation during 
the Tenth Five Year Plan. In the context of the announcement made by the 
Hon'ble Prime Minister for generating 50 million additional jobs in the country 
during this period, the SSI sector has t)een assigned the task of creating 4.4 
million additional jobs.

Threat posed to Dolphins in Chilka Lake 
MISS MABEL REBELLO (Madhya Pradesh): Madam, tourist boats in 
Chilka lake of Orissa are causing a se rious threat to the life of dolphins. 
According to the Wildlife Society of Orissa, 11 dolphins were killed during the 
last two years. Two dolphins were killed last month. Recognised as an 
endangered specie, the Irrawady dolphins (Orcealla Brevirostris). numbering 
55 are a unique natural heritage of Orissa, Chilka lake is one of the only two 
places in the world where these mammals are seen, the other being Songkhia 
lake in Thailand. 
Propellers of tourist boats kill or  seriously injure these dolphins 
whenever boats surround them. Curious t ourists always want to have a closer 
look at this rare mammal. With t he promotion of tour ism by the State 
Government, there has been a quantum jump in the number of tourists visiting 
Chilka, especially in winter. But, the tourism sans necessary precautions. It is 
becoming an encroachment on the rights of these animals. 
In view of their endangered status, these dolphins should receive the 
highest level of protection under law. It is true that tourism earns revenue for 
the country. But, at the same time, preserving our natural wealth and heritage 
should not be compromised with money, The Government should go in for 
projects like eco-tourism, which has been successfully experimented in Kerala. 
218 

[5 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA  
Since dolphins are endangered and rare species of mammals, I 
appeal to the Government to presen/e these nature-friendly animals for th6 
posterity, by doing everything possible,  even if it amounts to losing some 
money by way of tourism.

SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA (Rajasthan): Madam Deputy Chairman. 
I thank you for giving me this opportunity  to speak. Madam, I rise to speak on 
the Special Mention with regard to givi ng special status to Rajasthan, under 
the Accelerated Irrigation Benefit Progr amme. Madam, the Ministry of Water 
Resources has placed Jammu and Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh and the North-
Eastern States under special category for the development of water resources. 
These States are entitled to liberal norms for the Central Loan Assistance 
under the Accelerated Irrigation Benefit Programme, 
The norms of the Central Loan Assistance cover only the hilly 
regions, the backwardness or the terrorist-proneness. However, Rajasthan 
faces far more severe conditions than these special-category States. Two-
thirds of the State is desert, and ever y.year, it is declared the drought-prone 
State. Major part of the State is in the tribal belt, most backward in comparison 
to other States. Because of the international border, there is a constant threat 
of war. Furthermore, every year, some calamity strikes the State. 
In order to exploit the water potentia l available in the State, the State 
is in the process of identifying and executing various major, medium and minor 
irrigation schemes. The geographical draw back of the State has restrained its 
major and medium projects to go through. However, more and

Enhancement of royalty on lignite at par with group-Vcoal 
SHR! R. KAMARAJ fTarnil Nadu): Madam Deputy Chairman, my 
Special Mention is about tlie royalty on Neyveli lignite. The Government of 
India, in the Ministry of Energy, Department of Coal, decided in August, 1990, 
to pay royalty on lignite, by treating it  on par with Group V Coal. Therefore, the 
royalty for group V coal as well as lignite was fixed at Rs.2.50 per tonne. 
However, when the Government of Indi a raised the royalty on Group V coal to 
Rs. 25 per tonne in 1991, and to Rs. 50 per tonne in 1994, the royalty on lignite 
remained at Rs. 2.50 per tonne. The Tamil Nadu Government had repeatedly 
urged the Government of India to trea t the State on par wit h the other States 
that are benefited from the periodic revisi on of royalty, and made it clear that 
Tamil Nadu felt discriminated against by the retention of the old royalty rate, 
when the royalty on coal of equal parity had been increased twice. Finally, in 
March, 2001, the Ministry of Coal increas ed the royalty on lignite to Rs. 50 per 
tonne, but with prospective effect. The Neyveli Lignite Corporation was asked 
to pay to the Government of Tamil Nadu Rs.250 crores as a special 
dispensation against non-revision of royalty since 1993, which was recoverable 
from the royalty paid over the next thre e years. However, in March. 2001, by 
restoring parity for lignite to the levels of Grade V coal, as it was in 1991, the 
Government of India has not accounted fo r the revisions in royalty that were 
made much earlier for Grave V coal. If those rates are applied to lignite, 
Rs.541.29 crores is due to Tamil Nadu from 1990 to March 31, 2000. Hence, I 
request the Government to consider gi ving retrospective effect to royalty 
revisions for lignite on par with Grade V coal, and order release of Rs.54i.29  
crores, as arrears of royalty. Thank you, Madam.

SHRI EDUAROO FALEIRO (Goa) : M adam, Deputy Chairman, over ' 
the last few decades, India had taken steps to become self-reliant in , armaments 
and established an R&D organisation and a Defence Industry to back it up. 
Indeed, unless we attain substantial ca pability for indigenous manufacture of 
military equipment, we will be independent only in name and our foreign and 
defence policies will remain hostage to nations and transnationals that supply us 
with the wherewithal of Defence. -Yet, Madam, steps taken during the last 50 
years towards self-reliance in Defence are now being seriously compromised. 
The Navy had prepared a 30-Year Submarine Building Plan which was intended 
to beat the "de facto" Submarine Technology Control Regime as well as revive 
building activities at the Mazagon Docks so that we become a genuine submarine 
building nation. The proposal was to build  20 submarines at an approximate cost 
of Rs. 15,000 crore over a period upto 2025. The Submarine building would be 
done in Mumbai and Vizag in a consortium with Indian firms like Larsen and 
Toubro, BHEL etc. with whom the Navy had detailed techno-commercial 
discussions. The indigenous submarine design known as 'Project 75 India' was 
finalised in 1997-98 by our Naval Submarine Design Bureau. 
However, the Ministry of Defenc e has now announced an agreement 
to purchase 6 Scorpene Class Submarines. The Scorpene Submarine is 
neither cost-effective nor fulfils the military - effectiveness criteria for a 
resource constrained country and is h ugely expensive. The whole deal is 
reported to cost the public excheque r a sum of Rs.12,500 crores for six 
SKD/CKD kits intended for assembly at Mazagon Docks, when the entiVe cost 
of the 20 submarines to be made under Project 75 India on both coasts was 
budgeted for Rs. 15,(300 crores, Govern ment must disclose the reasons for 
the Scorpene deal.

Menace of ragging in the Country 
PROF, M. SANKARALINGAM (Tamil Nadu) : Madam, Deputy 
Chairman, the menace of ragging has raised its ugly head yet again in New 
Delhi: I am sure that this is not confined to any particular college in New Delhi. 
It is a regular and recurring feature in innumerable colleges all over the 
country, where freshers are humiliated and tortured by the seniors. These 
incidents invariably end up in tragic incidents like some freshers committing 
suicide and in a recent incident, two freshers going deaf. 
Recently, the Supreme Court of I ndia has warned that if educational 
institutions fail to curb ragging, its affili ations to the universities and financial 
aid could be withdrawn. The Government should set high standards to be 
followed by the seniors in treating freshe rs and should issue st rict instructions 
to be followed by the colleges / educationa l institutions to monitor the seniors 
as to whether they are indulging in ragging with a view to harassing the 
freshers, which results in unwanted heartburn and unwarranted hatred among 
seniors and juniors. 
It is high time, the Government should ban 'ragging' in colleges / 
educational institutions so that freshers are relieved of ragging by seniors in 
future. Here, I would like to  stress that the senior students of the Santosh 
Medical College, Ghaziabad, whose alleged ragging which has led to two 
freshers going deaf should not be al lowed to go scot-free. Many a time, 
incidents of ragging by seniors go unnoticed or do not come to light. Because 
the freshers take the ragging by seniors lying down, these types of incident 
continue till another incident catches the headlines in the newspapers. 
Therefore, I urge upon the Government to bring forward a stringent 
legislation and take all necessary steps to put an end to these activities. once 
for all.
